The City of Chicago continues to advance its 2022 Climate Action Plan (CAP), developed using the C40 Deadline 2020 framework and aligned with the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act (CEJA). The plan prioritizes workforce development, energy justice investments, and a transition to a renewable energy economy.

In 2023, analysis of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) suggested that Chicago could surpass its 2040 emissions reduction target. However, recent federal rollbacks—such as the weakening of clean energy tax incentives under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and the U.S. EPA's proposed revocation of its endangerment finding for vehicle-related greenhouse gas emissions—pose serious risks to the pace and scale of progress. Despite diminished federal support, Chicago remains steadfast in its climate goals and continues to lead with policies rooted in equity, science, and resilience.

column39: The Essex Climate Action Commission (ECAC) developed a net zero trajectory for Essex to 2050, based on current best thinking and the Commission's recommendations. This shows how we need to reduce our carbon emissions if we are to achieve net zero by 2050. Essex County Council (ECC) has committed to track the county's emissions against this trajectory every year, to gauge performance and ensure that the ambitions stated in Everyone's Essex strategy, to encourage, accelerate, and ensure a smooth transition to renewable energy and decarbonisation, are being met. We have historically tracked the county's emissions using a tool called Scatter - Setting City Area Targets and Trajectories for Emissions Reductions. It has recently been announced that this tool will no longer be updated, so whilst we have continued to use certain figures in our submission - Scope 3, for example - we have also developed an in-house tool that replicates the framework and data sources used within Scatter. This in-house resource allows ECC to continue to compare the overall and sector wide emissions against the Essex Climate Action Commission emissions trajectory to net zero. . When we set this target, our most recent actual figure was from 2020 (8.42 MtCO2e) which is 0.48 MtCO2e above target. Our aspiration for 2030 is that we will reduce our emissions from 8.42MtCO2e to 3.19 MtCO2e. This target was introduced in 2023 to complement our CN28 target (Target 1). The CH4 emissions data has a 2 year lag, and the 2023 emissions (published in 2025) are included here. Between 2018 and 2023, Nottingham's methane emissions have increased by 11%.

column39: The UK Government has made a commitment to reach net zero emissions by 2050. aligned to the goal of limiting global average temperature rise to 1.5 degrees. Our jurisdiction is aiming for the same goal but by the more ambitious date of 2030. There are various estimates of the extent to which UK local authorities can influence emissions for their areas, but typically estimated at around 30% - but either way the achievement of 'net zero' will be dependent on private action/resources and government action/resources outside the control of local authorities. This is why we use the UK national DESNZ data subset on 'emissions within the scope of influence of local authorities' to calculate our baseline and progress towards net zero as our headline measure of progress as it most closely reflects the emissions which we can influence. Our target covers all emissions included in this DESNZ dataset and by this metric, Reading achieved a 54% reduction in emissions between 2005 and 2022, the 12th largest reduction out of almost 400 UK local authorities. The 2022 figure of 54% represents a welcome reduction in emissions compared to the 2021 figure of 51% and a return to a downwards trajectory after emissions 'bounced-back' in 2021 following the lifting of pandemic restrictions. Reading's relative performance remains strong, as explained above, and our per capita emissions also remain the lowest of the 6 local authorities in the Berkshire region. The full subset of the main DESNZ dataset is available at https://view.officeapps.live.com/op/view.aspx?src=https%3A%2F%2Fassets.publishing.service.gov.uk%2Fmedia%2F667ad5b45b0d63b556a4b305%2F2005-22-uk-local-authority-ghg-emissions.xlsx&wdOrigin=BROWSELINK- see tab 2.1 and search 'Reading'

column39: The net-zero emissions in 2050 target was set as part of the declaration of the Climate Emergency by City Council in 2019 and the adoption of the Climate Emergency Action Plan in 2020, with an interim target of a 50% of 2007 emissions by 2030 (these re-affirmed emissions reduction targets set in a previous strategy in 2017). These emissions reduction targets are compliant with IPCC-recommended emissions pathways for 1.5 degC. Many components of the City's GHG reductions will be conditional on involvement from senior levels of government. Examples of these changes and priorities include: right-to-charge rules for electric vehicle owners in multi-unit residential buildings, ride-hailing legislation that aligns with zero emissions principles and complements sustainable travel, supporting the 'All On Board' campaign, accelerated transit electrification, a bold vision for the Regional Transportation Strategy, energy performance benchmarking for buildings, counting district energy systems with heat from renewable energy as a contributor towards the targets in BC's new renewable gas standard, and electricity pricing that supports electrification. At implementation level, the City will seek to leverage opportunities from existing Federal and Provincial programs, rather than developing standalone programs (e.g., pilot projects in partnership with the provincial government to retrofit affordable market rental housing and non-market housing). The City's Climate Emergency Action Plan (CEAP) and the province's CleanBC will contribute to reducing Vancouver's emissions from a baseline of 2.8 million tonnes in 2007 to below 1.4 million tonnes by 2030. To achieve this goal, the most stringent mix of policies must be adopted at both the City and provincial level. It should be noted that these policies work together, in addition to market changes, and technological adoption, as well as federal policies not explicitly modelled. The City conducted initial modelling showing that it would be able to meet its targets in 2020. The policy context changed by 2022, so the City conducted updated modelling in 2022 to measure the City's progress with the suite of policies it has implemented, has decided not to implement, and still needs to implement. This updated modelling indicates that if all proposed policies still to be adopted are implemented we can anticipate a 41% reduction in pollution in 2030 from 2007 levels, leaving us with an additional 9% points of pollution to reduce to achieve our 2030 targets. Modelling is being done in 2025-2026 to forecast the impact of CEAP and CleanBC policies on GHG emissions under several policy scenarios. Preliminary results indicate that we will need to identify additional policies to meet our 50% emissions reduction targets by 2030.

The carbon neutral target for Cardiff by 2030 was formally established in 2019, when Cardiff Council declared a Climate Emergency and began developing the One Planet Cardiff strategy. The strategy outlines the Council's commitment to:
1. Make Cardiff Council carbon neutral by 2030.
2. Work with partners to make Cardiff as a city carbon neutral by 2030.

Cardiff's territorial greenhouse gas emissions estimates in 2019 and 2023 are taken from the latest dataset of the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, which is two years in arrears (https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/uk-local-authority-and-regional-greenhouse-gas-emissions-statistics-2005-to-2023). 

Emissions in Cardiff declined by 14.71% from 2019 to 2023, falling from 1,818.7 Kt CO₂e to 1,551.1 Kt CO₂e. The most significant decrease came from the waste sector, which saw a 34.75% reduction, followed closely by industry (31.55%) and agriculture (25.20%). These reductions in Cardiff's greenhouse gas emissions between 2019 and 2023 demonstrate moderate but meaningful progress toward the city's net zero target by 2030.

In 2019 Glasgow declared a Climate and Ecological Emergency. Following this, extensive stakeholder engagement and consultation led to the creation of Glasgow's Climate Plan. There was a clear aspiration from all involved that Glasgow should lead the way in taking action to address climate change, culminating in agreeing the aspirational net zero carbon target of 2030 and an action to create a Routemap for the city. The Net Zero Routemap (NZRM) provides the scientific evidence to underpin the ambition set out in the Climate Plan and establishes a scientific basis for scenario planning that is both rigorous and flexible. The development of Glasgow's Net Zero Routemap includes the use of a software platform (ClimateView OS), which utilises data so that we can be agile as we work towards addressing the evolving challenge that climate change presents.

In advance of the work undertaken to model the different mitigation actions and their impact, an internationally recognised approach to Science Based Target assessment was undertaken using the D2020 method, replicating the approach taken by many other cities around the world. It was identified however that the ClimateViewOS platform provides a more robust science-based framework for setting carbon budgets for Glasgow's 2030 net zero target, primarily due to its transparency of data use and its ability to identify pathways per emissions sector. This aligns clearly with Scotland's National approach through the Scottish Climate Intelligence Service (SCIS) to roll out the use of the ClimateViewOS platform to all local authorities. The hierarchy used to assess the priority and planning of mitigation actions was assessed in line with the Climate Change Committee (CCC) Pathway to Net Zero priorities (https://www.theccc.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/CCC-Insights-Briefing-Determining-a-pathway-to-Net-Zero.pdf).

The NZRM development resulted in two pathways being modelled to meet the Council's 2030 net zero ambition, including limiting reliance on carbon capture and removals as much as possible. Both pathways are built using the same inventory data, but the type of mitigation action and the speed at which action happens differs between pathways:
> Projected Pathway: This pathway has been created based on projected emissions reductions associated with the ambition and commitment within the Council's current policies and strategies, alongside the National interim net zero targets of 75% reduction by 2030. Figure 2 below provides an overview of the contribution of the different emissions categories within this pathway. This pathway results in an approximate emissions reduction of 60%
> Accelerated Pathway: Within this pathway the boundaries of demand reduction and improved efficiencies have been pushed to their limits, based on the need for systemic change by 2030 and are recognised as highly ambitious and very challenging. This pathway limits reliance on carbon capture and removals as much as possible and results in an approximate emissions reduction of 80%.

Glasgow's CO2 emissions in 2023 totalled 21704 ktCO2; this represents a 6.2% reduction from the 2022 total of 23141 ktCO2 and a 49.3% reduction in emissions from the baseline year of 2006. This data demonstrates that policies and projects aimed at supporting Glasgow's transition to a net zero carbon city are having a positive impact. This data trajectory enables us to understand that our current pathway falls in the middle of our projected and accelerated pathway scenarios as outlined within the Net Zero Routemap.

Taking the highest reduction target of -15%, the estimated per capita greenhouse gas emissions for 2030 after reduction would be 17.28 metric tons. 3. Therefore, the emission reduction target for Kaohsiung City in 2030 (with the base year of 2005) is -27.40%. Toronto City Council adopted the Net Zero Strategy (NZS) in December 2021 which includes a target of net zero by 2040 and presents a set of 2030 interim targets for community-wide emissions as well as City of Toronto corporate targets to demonstrate leadership by example. Ιn August 2024, the City of Athens adopted the Climate City Contract. The Climate City Contract of Athens is partially based on the 2022 Climate Action Plan as well as on insights stemming from engagement activities during the last decade with stakeholders from Athens and the networks and initiatives that Athens belongs to. The CCC raises the ambition of the previous plan significantly, by bringing the target to climate neutrality from 2050 forward to 2030, along with an updated
set of objectives and a portfolio of actions to realise this target. The goal for climate neutrality by 2030 will be primarily achieved through extensive emissions cuts within all emissions-intensive sectors of the city, including energy supply, the built environment, transportation and mobility, and waste. In line with the climate neutrality definition pursued by the Cities Mission, the target for emissions cuts is set to 80% compared to a 'Business-as-Usual' scenario—i.e., assuming that the Municipality did not develop any further climate policy after 2019. The residual chunk of 20% of emissions will be covered through nature-based solutions, by expanding the city's green infrastructure and afforestation/reforestation activities in the region. The climate neutrality target covers all administrative territories within the Municipality and all emission sources, sectors, and relevant GHG emissions. While the most recent emissions inventory that was available at the time of its drafting was for 2022, in consultation with the Net Zero Cities advisors, it was decided to use as a base year the 2019 inventory to avoid any data
anomalies due to the impact of COVID-19. 

The CCC Action Plan includes an assessment of existing climate policies and the emissions gap
between the 2030 GHG reduction projected by existing policies and the climate neutrality goal
envisioned. To understand this gap in more detail, a reference scenario with no climate policy after 2019 was simulated ('Business as Usual') as well as a scenario that achieves an 80% emission reduction for the Municipality of Athens compared to the reference scenario. The simulation was done based on the
economic model of the NetZeroCities programme and with the guidance and support of its
advisors. 
 
It is worth clarifying that the GHG values that are calculated within the CCC Action Plan are based on the 'BASIC' reference level of the international
GHG protocol, GPC. The BASIC level used in the Action Plan includes Scope 1 and 2 emissions for the built environment and transport as well as emissions of all three Scopes for waste. So, in the case of Athens, emissions that are not taken into account at the BASIC level and therefore in
the objectives of the CCC are the GHG emissions due to electricity network losses (Scope 3 of the built environment) as well as half of the transboundary traffic through the Municipality of Athens (Scope 3 of transport). It is noted that the other half of transboundary traffic emissions are considered by assumption as Scope 1, based on the proposal of the C40 Cities network. Beyond the suggestion of the Net Zero Cities advisors to use the BASIC level, the remaining emissions are outside the jurisdiction of the Municipality of Athens, especially in the context of network losses. Nevertheless, the Municipality of
Athens will cooperate with neighboring municipalities within the framework of the Athens Energy Alliance in order to reduce emissions due to transboundary mobility beyond the share attributable to the Municipality of Athens.

Between 2024 and 2025, many projects have started such as the ASCEND project on 15-minute neighbourhoods and the municipal energy community which will eventually result in emissions reductions that will be seen in the coming years.

- BAU methodology explanation
An analysis of GHG emissions trajectories was made under the BAU scenario, which is a scenario with no GHG reduction activities in the boundary. GHG emissions trajectories were prepared by forecasting activity data in the future and multiplying with emission factors that are the same as the base year (the assumption is that the technology or process of greenhouse gas emission has the same characteristics). In the case of the BMA, GHG emissions trajectories were analyzed under the BAU scenario covering GHG emissions from the base year, 2018 to 2030. Forecasting of activity data in each sector depends on the availability of the data and the context of Bangkok. For the stationary energy and transportation sectors, forecasted activity data was inferred from historical activity data. In the waste sector, activity data was forecasted by gathering growth rates from relevant or responsible agencies, such as population growth. However, the BMA may work with the private sector to gather information on activities data and growth rates to estimate GHG emissions trajectories in the future that are more consistent with the context of Bangkok.The outbreak of Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) during 2020-2021 led to increased energy use in residential buildings but decreased energy use in commercial buildings, manufacturing industries, and transportation. However, this change is temporary due to a halt in some economic activities. Once Bangkok recovers from COVID-19, climate activities, as well as their growth rate, will turn back to normal. Bangkok's GHG emissions trajectories, therefore, have been analyzed based on its normal situation. column39: In the context of the revision of the Berlin Climate and Energy Act in 2021, Berlin's climate targets were updated. They were adjusted to the Paris standard and compiled based on scientific findings of the German Advisory Council on the Environment (Sachverständigenrat für Umweltfragen). According to the 2022 emission data, the CO2 emissions relevant for Berlin's climate protection targets amounted to a total of 15,984 thousand tonnes. Following the slump in emissions in the coronavirus year 2020, there was a renewed increase for the second year in a row. However, CO2 emissions are still well below the pre-pandemic level and 45.3% lower than in the base year 1990. The development of emissions in 2022 was significantly influenced by the effects of the Russian war of aggression on Ukraine and the intensified efforts to save energy in response to this. In addition, unusually mild winter weather had a dampening effect on heat demand and CO2 emissions . On the other hand, the carbon footprint of the electricity consumed in Berlin deteriorated - despite the growth of renewable energies - because gas capacities were replaced by more CO2-intensive coal throughout the country as a result of the crisis. Achieving the medium and long-term climate protection targets requires a high pace of climate action.

In 2023, total greenhouse gas emissions decreased by approximately 20% compared to 2005 levels, and by about a quarter compared to the peak in 2014.

Our four major decarbonisation strategies are “net-zero electricity generation”, “energy saving”, “green transport” and “waste reduction”. 

Net-zero electricity generation” -By 2035 or earlier, cease the use of coal for daily power generation; the expected completion of the reinforcement project of the clean energy transmission system in 2026, and the reservation of land in Area 132 of Tseung Kwan O for the construction of new power facilities, the capacity for electricity transmission from the Mainland to Hong Kong will be further enhanced, the proportion of zero-carbon energy in the electricity generation fuel mix will be increased to about 60% to 70% by 2035 or earlier; increase the proportion of renewable energy in the fuel mix for electricity generation to 7.5% to 10% by 2035 or earlier. The Environmental Protection Department (“EPD”) has commissioned three large-scale waste-to-energy facilities, namely T·PARK (sludge treatment facility), O·PARK1 (Organic Resources Recovery Centre Phase 1), and O·PARK2 (Organic Resources Recovery Centre Phase 2), and approved approximately HK$2.2 billion to implement about 260 small-scale government renewable energy projects, such as developing solar power systems at water facilities and landfills. To encourage the private sector to develop renewable energy, the government has introduced a Feed-in Tariff Scheme and various support measures, including assisting the private sector in installing solar power systems in outdoor parking lots and formulating suitable non-combustible fire safety requirements and standards for building-integrated solar power systems. As of December 2024, the Feed-in Tariff Scheme has received approximately 26 000 applications. Through the
aforementioned renewable energy projects, we expect to generate more than 500 million kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, reducing carbon emissions by about
540 000 tonnes.

“Energy saving and green buildings” - Commercial buildings to reduce 30-40% by 2050; residential buildings to reduce 20-30% by 2050, and to achieve half of the above targets by 2035 or earlier. Through multipronged energy-saving measures, we estimate that a total of about 3.7 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity was saved in 2024 compared to 2015, equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of about 1 million three-person households. 

(Cont)

“Green transport” -The proportion of electric private cars among newly registered private cars has increased from over 20% in 2021 to nearly 70% now, ranking among the top in the world. Currently, the number of electric vehicles (“EVs”) in Hong Kong has exceeded 110 000, and increased eightfold in five years. The government aims to set a clear target to cease the registration of new fuel and hybrid private cars by 2035 or earlier and increase the total number of parking spaces with charging infrastructure in Hong Kong to about 200 000 by mid-2027. For the green transition of commercial vehicles, the government published the Green Transformation Roadmap of Public Buses and Taxis in December 2024, with key measures including earmarking about HK$470 million to subsidise franchised bus operators to purchase about 600 electric buses and HK$135 million to subsidise taxi trade to purchase 3 000 electric taxis. With the implementation of net-zero electricity generation in future, the two subsidy schemes can reduce about 210 000 tonnes of carbon emissions annually. For electric public light buses, the government has earmarked HK$80 million to implement a pilot scheme to subsidise operators to purchase electric public light buses for trial, so as to
evaluate the feasibility of their application in Hong Kong. To promote hydrogen fuel cell (“HFC”) heavy vehicles, the first HFC double-deck bus commenced trial operation in November 2023 and started to provide passenger service in February 2024; the trial of the hydrogen fuelled light rail vehicle was completed at the end of 2024; and three HFC street washing vehicles of the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department commenced trial operation in June 2025. In the field of green aviation, the Airport Authority Hong Kong (“AAHK”) has committed to increasing the number of electric vehicles at Hong Kong International Airport to 3 000 and providing more than 1,320 charging points to support airport operations by the end of 2030, and plans to increase the number of electric ground services equipment (“GSE”) from the existing 500 units to about 1 000 units, with at least 95% being electric GSE, making Hong Kong International Airport the first international airport to adopt GSE Pooling on such a large-scale. In the maritime sector, the government has promulgated the “Action Plan for Green Maritime Fuel Bunkering”, setting a multi-fuel strategy, with an aim to develop Hong Kong into a green maritime fuel bunkering and trading centre. The Pilot Scheme for Electric Ferries is also actively being implemented, with the first electric ferry “Xin Ming Zhu XXXIX” commencing passenger service in March 2025. The second electric ferry “Hong Kong Water Taxi 28” also began trial in May 2025. In addition, three hybrid ferries under the Vessel Subsidy Scheme progressively commenced trial at the end of December 2024. The government is also studying the introduction of onshore power supply facilities at the Kai Tak Cruise Terminal to support the low-carbon transformation of the international cruise industry.

 ”Waste reduction” -The amount of municipal solid waste disposal in Hong Kong has shown a downward trend, with daily per capita disposal decreasing from 1.53 kg in 2021 to 1.40 kg in 2024, while the overall recycling rate increased from 31% in 2021 to 33% in 2023, indicating that citizens' environmental awareness and recycling habits are gradually improving. The government will continue developing waste-to-energy facilities and promoting waste reduction and recycling, which can help achieve “zero landfill” by 2035.

Para lograr la meta global de limitar el incremento de la temperatura promedio por debajo de 1.5C, la Ciudad de México debe transitar a la neutralidad de emisiones y descarbonizar la economía. La transición necesaria para colocar a la ciudad en línea con las metas globales se analiza mediante dos escenarios de emisiones que buscan representar distintos niveles de ambición en su reducción:
-Escenario de mitigación actual o no condicionado, que representa los programas, medidas y proyectos que se pondrán en marcha desde la Ciudad de México con recursos propios y no condicionados al apoyo internacional o a financiamiento climático adicional.
-Escenario ambicioso de cero emisiones, que si bien está alineado con una trayectoria de reducción de emisiones acorde a la meta global de 1.5ºC, se encuentra condicionado a la cooperación técnica internacional, el acceso a recursos financieros adicionales y a la transferencia tecnológica.

En este sentido, dentro de la Estrategia Local de Acción Climática 2021-2050 y el Programa de Acción Climática 2021-2030, se plantean medidas para reducir y capturar el 24% de las emisiones de CGEI para el 2030 respecto a la línea base de 2016. Con ello, alinea las acciones climáticas con otros instrumentos legales y de planeación sectoriales con el potencial de contribuir a los compromisos de la política climática y ambiental de la Ciudad. Las metas están establecidas en el capítulo 'EMISIONES DE COMPUESTOS Y GASES DE EFECTO INVERNADERO (CGEI)' en el apartado de 'ESCENARIO CONDICIONADO O DE CERO EMISIONES' del documento adjunto.

Para lograr la meta global de limitar el incremento de la temperatura promedio por debajo de 1.5C, la Ciudad de México debe transitar a la neutralidad de emisiones y descarbonizar la economía. La transición necesaria para colocar a la ciudad en línea con las metas globales se analiza mediante dos escenarios de emisiones que buscan representar distintos niveles de ambición en su reducción:
-Escenario de mitigación actual o no condicionado, que representa los programas, medidas y proyectos que se pondrán en marcha desde la Ciudad de México con recursos propios y no condicionados al apoyo internacional o a financiamiento climático adicional.
-Escenario ambicioso de cero emisiones, que si bien está alineado con una trayectoria de reducción de emisiones acorde a la meta global de 1.5ºC, se encuentra condicionado a la cooperación técnica internacional, el acceso a recursos financieros adicionales y a la transferencia tecnológica.

En este sentido, dentro de la Estrategia Local de Acción Climática 2021-2050 y el Programa de Acción Climática 2021-2030, se plantean medidas para reducir y capturar el 32% de las emisiones de CGEI para el 2024 respecto a la línea base de 2016. Con ello, alinea las acciones climáticas con otros instrumentos legales y de planeación sectoriales con el potencial de contribuir a los compromisos de la política climática y ambiental de la Ciudad. Las metas están establecidas en el capítulo 'EMISIONES DE COMPUESTOS Y GASES DE EFECTO INVERNADERO (CGEI)' en el apartado de 'ESCENARIO CONDICIONADO O DE CERO EMISIONES' del documento adjunto.

column39:
City of Paris adopted in 2018 a carbon neutrality pathway for 2050 which aims zero emissions for local emissions and net zero for the territory's overall carbon footprint. Local emissions consist of residential and tertiary buildings, inner transport, industry and waste emissions. Outside emissions consist of upstream energy, construction and material, food, outside transport (passenger and freight) and air travel (passenger and freight) emissions. The carbon footprint consists of both local and outside emissions together. 

The 2004 baseline is the City's first greenhouse gas inventory. The 2050 targets relative to this baseline thus are -100% for local emissions and -80% for the carbon footprint, leaving a remaining 20% (quantified at 5,67 MtCO2e in the 2024-2030 Climate Action Plan), currently deemed incompressible (mainly air travel), to be compensated by all local actors. 

The City set 2030 intermediary targets for both perimeters : -50% for local emissions and -40% for the overall territory carbon footprint relative to the 2004 baseline. In 2022, assessed emissions represented a 32% reduction to the 2004 baseline. (https://www.paris.fr/pages/paris-pour-le-climat-2148)

In July 2025, the current French NDC is 40% of domestic GHG reductions by 2030 compared to 1990. As such, the Parisian intermediary target represents a more ambitious target in a reduced span of time.

2025 change note : the baseline for local emissions was corrected as 7,42 MtCO2e, in accordance with the official baseline published in the Climate Action Plan 2024-2030. The 0,02 MtCO2e variance is due to recalculations.

The 2050 targets relative to this baseline thus are -100% for local emissions and -80% for the carbon footprint, leaving a remaining 20% (quantified at 5,67 MtCO2e in the 2024-2030 Climate Action Plan), currently deemed incompressible (mainly air travel), to be compensated by all local actors. 

The City set 2030 intermediary targets for both perimeters : -50% for local emissions and -40% for the overall territory carbon footprint relative to the 2004 baseline. In 2022, assessed emissions represented a 32% reduction to the 2004 baseline. (https://www.paris.fr/pages/paris-pour-le-climat-2148)

In July 2025, the current French NDC is 40% of domestic GHG reductions by 2030 compared to 1990. As such, the Parisian intermediary target represents a more ambitious target in a reduced span of time.

Objetivo de Mitigación: Aumentar el reciclaje de residuos orgánicos, mediante la separación, tratamiento y valorización de residuos orgánicos.

La disposición de residuos en rellenos sanitarios está en directa relación con el crecimiento de la población, por lo que se espera que las emisiones continúen en aumento a menos que se implementen medidas de captura de metano o de valorización de residuos orgánicos. Por otra parte, la implementación de esta medida permite disminuir el volumen de residuos enviados a sitios de disposición final y extender la vida útil de los mismos.

column39: Based on prior commitments, the CAP development process originally contemplated net-zero emissions by 2045 as the overall target. More recently, legislation sponsored by Mayor London Breed that updated Chapter 9 of the Environment Code accelerated the net-zero goal to 2040 and it also specifies net-zero as a 90% reduction below San Francisco's baseline year of 1990 with the remaining 10% of GHG emissions being sequestered through nature-based solutions. Current projections show that if all the strategies in the 2021 CAP were implemented based on the specified timelines, San Francisco would see an approximate 80% reduction from 1990 levels by 2040, an 87% reduction by 2045, and a 94% reduction by 2050. Peer review by external technical experts concluded the 2021 CAP puts forth an exhaustive set of strategies, and indicated that the main way to achieve the 2040 net-zero goal would be to accelerate implementation. City staff-led technical working groups affirmed that the proposed strategies had already considered aggressive implementation timelines, and any further acceleration would be possible only with significant assistance and support from external entities. Initial solutions to the projected 2040 shortfall include: receiving large amounts of heavily subsidized capital from non-city sources, aligned transformative policies from the state and federal government, and tapping into new science and tools to quantify the carbon sequestration effects of Healthy Ecosystems strategies, which are currently not accounted for within the emissions reduction projections.\n\nSan Francisco is currently updating the CAP and will be evaluating the reduction strategies needed to reach net-zero by 2040.

In 2009 Warsaw joined the European Commission's initiative Covenant of Mayors - 31 August 2021 the Warsaw City Council has adopted Position No. 37 on a new climate declaration as part of the international initiative 'Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy'. It obliges the Capital City of Warsaw to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in accordance with the goal of achieving climate neutrality in 2050, to increase the city's resilience and adaptation to the adverse effects of climate change, and to combat fuel poverty as one of the key actions to ensure a just transition.
Warsaw has become a participant in the European Union Mission - 100 Climate Neutral and Smart Cities, which aims to achieve climate neutrality by 2030. Participating in the Mission constitutes a great challenge for the city and a motivation for even more intensive measures than those envisaged so far in Warsaw's Green Vision (Green Cities and Climate Action Plan) - the city's main document describing pathways to climate neutrality by 2050 at the latest.
When joining the EU Mission '100 climate-neutral and smart cities by 2030', Warsaw declared to setting a reduction target of 80% by 2030 for two city districts. This decision was driven by an awareness of local and systemic possibilities and limitations, which is explained in detail later in the document.
Participating in the Mission and preparing the Climate City Contract, implemented in two selected districts: Praga-Południe and Ursynów mobilise for implementing innovations and bold solutions that will allow achieving climate neutrality in all key sectors of the city's functioning and that can, once tested in the above-mentioned districts, be implemented throughout the city.

Taipei City aligns with the outcomes of the UNFCCC Conference of the Parties (COP) and follows the IPCC 1.5°C pathway by committing to a science-based target (SBT) of reducing emissions 40% by 2030 from a 2005 baseline. This ambition exceeds Taiwan's national target of 28±2% by 2030 and demonstrates the City's commitment to global climate leadership. Taipei has also pledged Net Zero emissions by 2050, with 2030 identified as a critical milestone. Guided by its 2050 Net Zero Pathway, the City translates global climate commitments into actionable, sector-specific policies:
1. Building Sector: Implementation of mandatory energy efficiency inventories and disclosure, with all new buildings required to achieve Class 1 or higher energy efficiency standards. Transit-Oriented Development (TOD), public housing, and municipal projects are adopting zero-carbon lifecycle design, while pilot applications of hydrogen fuel cells and a Tokyo-modeled emissions trading system are being advanced.
2. Transportation Sector: Targeting a 70% green transport modal share by 2030. Measures include the full electrification of the public bus fleet, 35% of new motorcycles to be electric, expansion of shared mobility (24,400 vehicles) and public bicycles (13,240 bikes / 543 km lanes), completion of the MRT loop, and the installation of 2,000 EV charging points and 576 smart intersections.
3. Waste Sector: Achieving a 70% resource recovery rate by 2030 through bans on single-use plastics and disposable tableware, expanding circular container systems, reaching 94% sewage treatment coverage, and transforming incinerators into green energy plants and circular economy parks.
Progress toward these targets is monitored under the UN SDGs framework, reported through Taipei's Voluntary Local Reviews (VLRs), and aligned with CDP's emphasis on transparent, science-based climate action.

Taipei City has adopted a science-based target (SBT) to reduce GHG emissions by 65% by 2040 compared to 2005 levels, positioning this milestone between the City's 2030 (40%) and 2050 net zero commitments. The target aligns with the IPCC 1.5°C pathway and the City's 2050 Net Zero Roadmap, ensuring continuity and ambition beyond national benchmarks.
Key strategies will be implemented across three sectors:
1. Building Sector: By 2040, all new buildings must comply with Class 1+ energy efficiency standards, with expanded deployment of renewable energy and hydrogen fuel cells.
2. Transportation Sector: Green transport share will reach 75%, with 50% electrification of private vehicles and the introduction of commercial electric trucks and hydrogen-powered vehicles. Shared mobility will expand to 25,850 vehicles, the public bike system to 16,000 units and 596 km of lanes, alongside 10,000 EV charging spaces and 1,480 smart intersections.
3. Waste Sector: The recycling rate will rise to 75%, wastewater treatment coverage to 97%, supported by organic waste co-digestion for power generation, new green power plants, and adoption of CCUS technologies.
Progress will be monitored under the UN SDGs framework and disclosed through Taipei's Voluntary Local Reviews (VLRs), reinforcing transparency and alignment with CDP's focus on science-based climate targets.

column39:
Taipei City has committed to a science-based long-term target to achieve 100% GHG reduction by 2050 compared to 2005 levels, reaching net zero emissions. This target aligns with the IPCC 1.5°C pathway, the IEA Net Zero Roadmap, and global best practices, positioning the City ahead of national commitments. Under the BAU scenario, Taipei would emit 12.26 million tCO₂e by 2050, which highlights the urgent need for a comprehensive cross-sector transformation. Guided by scientific methodologies, the City has systematically assessed climate risks and impacts, and will drive the transition through robust governance frameworks and concrete actions.
The City's net zero strategy is driven by three major pathways, complemented by enhanced carbon sinks and emerging zero/negative-carbon technologies:
1. Building Sector - Smart Zero-Carbon Buildings: By 2050, all new, commercial, and public buildings must meet Class 1+ energy efficiency standards, using at least 55% renewable or hydrogen energy, while general buildings must use at least 20%. Existing buildings will undergo mandatory energy audits and retrofits, with public buildings renovated at 3% of total floor area annually.
2. Transportation Sector - Green and Low-Carbon Mobility: By 2050, 80% of trips will be made via green transportation. Private vehicles will be 95% electrified, with large-scale adoption of hydrogen and commercial EV fleets. Shared mobility will expand to 27,500 vehicles, and the public bike system to 21,500 units with 596 km of lanes. Low-carbon zones will cover the entire city, restricting high-carbon vehicles.
3. Waste Sector - Total Recycling and Zero Waste: By 2050, the resource recovery rate will reach 80% and wastewater treatment coverage 98%. Incinerators will be transformed into green power plants, integrated with facilities for food waste, bottom ash, and resource recovery to form a circular energy park. Advanced CCUS technologies will be deployed to eliminate residual emissions.

This 2050 net zero target is designed as the culmination of the City's SBT-aligned trajectory—40% by 2030, 65% by 2040, and 100% by 2050—ensuring coherence with central government policies on renewable energy, hydrogen, and electric mobility, while keeping flexibility for technological innovation.

column39: Our mid-term greenhouse gas emissions reduction target is to achieve a 63% reduction in total jurisdiction-wide emissions by 2030 compared to 2018 levels, aligned with the WWF One Planet City Challenge (OPCC) methodology. This goal was formally established in 2019 and represents a crucial stepping-stone toward our net zero 2050 pathway. The target covers all BASIC+ GPC emissions sources, ensuring that direct emissions (scope 1), indirect energy-related emissions (scope 2), and significant waste, industrial processes, and AFOLU-related sources (scope 3) are fully included. By adopting this boundary, we ensure that the target is transparent, complete, and compliant with the Global Covenant of Mayors (GCoM) Mitigation Pillar requirements. The gases covered include CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O, which together account for more than 95% of our emissions profile. HFCs, PFCs, SF₆, and NF₃ are also monitored where material, in line with IPCC and UNFCCC guidance. The methodology behind the target is rooted in science-based pathways consistent with limiting global warming to 1.5°C, ensuring fairness and equity by reflecting both historical responsibilities and current economic development levels. This approach is designed to support alignment with the Paris Agreement and our country's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC). To track progress, we conduct annual GHG inventories, verified and updated using CIRIS tables and IPCC 2006 Guidelines, which provide robust datasets and comparability with international standards. Monitoring involves collaboration between municipal agencies, universities, and local utilities to ensure accuracy. As of the most recent inventory, we have already achieved a reduction of approximately 25% from the 2018 baseline, demonstrating moderate progress. A portfolio of actions underpins this trajectory: scaling renewable energy in electricity generation, retrofitting municipal and private buildings to improve energy efficiency, electrifying public and private transport fleets, implementing sustainable mobility strategies (bike lanes, pedestrianization, e-mobility infrastructure), and improving solid waste management with methane capture. Importantly, no carbon credits are planned for this target, ensuring that all reductions are achieved through real, in-boundary decarbonization measures. Financial support is partly derived from national programs and EU green funding instruments, while public-private partnerships accelerate deployment of clean technologies. The conditionality of the target rests on strong national support, particularly through renewable energy subsidies, decarbonization of the national electricity grid, and legislation supporting low-emission transport and energy efficiency standards. Co-benefits include improved air quality, reduced fossil fuel imports, enhanced energy security, and job creation in the green economy. Community engagement is also central, with citizens involved in energy-saving campaigns, awareness programs, and participatory budgeting for climate initiatives. Overall, this mid-term target is both ambitious and realistic, ensuring we remain on a credible trajectory toward our 2050 net zero goal.

column39: Our long-term greenhouse gas emissions reduction target is to reach Net Zero by 2050, which means reducing emissions by 100% compared to the 2018 base year and neutralizing any remaining residual emissions with high-integrity carbon removals or credits. This target was established in 2019 and has been designed to be fully science-based, again using the WWF OPCC methodology. The boundary of this target covers the entire jurisdiction (same as reported in section 1.2), including all BASIC+ GPC emissions categories: energy, transport, waste, industrial processes, and AFOLU. The gases covered include CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O as core categories, alongside monitoring and reduction strategies for F-gases (HFCs, PFCs, SF₆, NF₃) to ensure no significant sources are overlooked. This comprehensive inclusion makes the target transparent, equitable, and compliant with the Integrity Matters criteria for credible net zero targets. Monitoring is carried out through our jurisdiction-wide GHG inventory, updated annually, and supplemented by sectoral progress indicators such as renewable energy share, building retrofits completed, public transport electrification rates, and waste diversion from landfill. By 2050, we anticipate a small proportion of residual emissions (estimated at 10%), largely from hard-to-abate sectors such as cement production, aviation, and some agricultural activities. These emissions will be addressed through carbon dioxide removals (e.g., afforestation, soil carbon sequestration, biochar, and potentially direct air capture where feasible) or offset through high-quality, externally verified carbon credits that meet strict integrity standards. Conditional elements of this target include national-level policies, such as the full decarbonization of the national grid, successful deployment of carbon capture and storage (CCS) technologies, and scaling of innovative low-carbon solutions in industry and aviation. Financial and technical support from the national government, the EU, and international climate finance instruments will be critical to achieving this. Progress so far has been encouraging: emissions have been reduced by 25% from the 2018 baseline, renewable energy capacity has increased by 45%, and green transport systems are being expanded. The co-benefits of pursuing net zero by 2050 are substantial: improved public health through cleaner air, energy cost savings, climate resilience, biodiversity enhancement through nature-based solutions, and long-term economic competitiveness. Public participation and transparent governance are central to the success of this strategy, ensuring accountability and trust. This net zero goal also sends a strong signal to businesses, investors, and citizens that our jurisdiction is committed to a just and equitable climate transition, aligned with the Paris Agreement and global climate justice principles. Ultimately, the 2050 target embodies our vision of a sustainable, resilient, and inclusive future for all residents.

Alignment with national targets: SA's 1st NDC proposed an emissions trajectory in bands derived from an extensive study in 2010. This trajectory envelope became known the “peak plateau and decline” profile and implied that the country's emissions would peak between 2025 & 2035 but within a large 200 Mt band. The 1st NDC was updated in 2021 which set a peak for emissions in 2025 and considerably narrowed the band of uncertainty also lowering the lower limit of the target range for 2030. The 2nd NDC is currently in a public commentary process and extends the trajectory envelope to 2035, narrowing the band of uncertainty from 70 Mt to 60 MT. These bands imply a wide range of possible absolute reduction between 2025 & 2035 of 5% - 37% and will depend on actual emissions in 2025. Furthermore, population growth in SA cities is significantly higher (2%) compared to the national average (1.3%). Direct comparison with the City's voluntary target therefore requires a per capita analysis in bands. National emissions were 482 Mt CO2e in 2017 which, given the 2030 NDC commitments of between 420 & 350 Mt CO2e in 2030, implies a 13-27% absolute drop. At the national average population growth rate this is a 27 - 39% per capita drop whereas the City's target, assuming 2% population growth rate is a 31% per capita drop. The City's target voluntary target for 2030 therefore falls within the per capita range of the national target and is in-line with the national ambition.
Conditional components: While the emissions trajectory of the City is on track for the target, several factors relating to national policy and market trends, will determine whether the targets will be met. Due to national legislation, the City does not have full control over some key intervention areas. Several amendments to the national Electricity Regulations over recent years have opened up opportunities for the City to play a role in securing and decarbonising its energy supply. While the City has procurement processes underway to purchase electricity from IPPs and is expanding its own modest utility scale generation assets, these processes have been challenging and have many attendant business and regulatory risks. The nature of the national power system, the many reforms notwithstanding, means a reliance on coal-intensive grid power for some time to come. A wholesale electricity market is however scheduled to begin trading in April 2026.
The rail service within Cape Town is managed by national state-owned entities or regional government contractors, limiting the potential for significant improvements or expansions to the services required to accelerate modal shift in transport. Proposed amendments to the National Land Transport Act may however devolve the full public transport mandate to the local government to act as a Transport Authority and concessionaire of rail. In 2023/24 the national rail utility also made progress in restoring service to most lines investing in tracks, stations and rolling stock. Roughly half of the collection of solid waste within the city is handled by private companies, making the monitoring and regulation of waste diversion to landfill a challenge. Buildings are a key sector in the new action plan and there is a dedicated NZC buildings program in place. Integration of new building stock into spatial planning frameworks is also essential to make public transport work. Most building stock is however constructed by private developers and a recessionary business environment with low confidence makes regulation unpopular and political traction low at this time. 
Progress: The requirements for shifts in the electricity sector depend on transport and waste emissions. If emissions from these two sectors increase modestly or decline slightly, it is estimated that attaining the target will require a net 10% EE improvement, combined with 7% of clean electricity supply (from locally procured or produced renewable generation, including SSEG). Population indexed growth in transport and waste emissions would however either require higher EE of 22% or a higher renewable electricity share of 20%. The foundation of the City's direct contribution to this 2030 target is through enabling the supply of renewable electricity from 250 MW of utility scale solar PV capacity either procured by the City or wheeled to customers. These projects are now spread across construction, contracting and planning stage. The severity of load-shedding between 2021 & 2023 drove exponential growth in private solar PV systems. This could potentially lead to the City attaining 15-20% renewable electricity share in the medium term, subject to overcoming regulatory constraints. The City has also begun construction of an ambitious expansion of its My-Citi bus network. At this stage there reason to be optimistic that the load-shedding crisis, (currently in abeyance) has driven an outcome where the interim target is exceeded even if transport & waste emissions increase.

The City's carbon neutral scenario modelling utilised the C40 Pathways Tool. Scenarios under optimistic and pessimistic conditions were modelled and informed the target reported here. The C40 Deadline 2020 Framework classified member cities according to socio-economic conditions and development status. Cape Town was classified as a “Late-peaking developing city” and for the time being is not required to mitigate “residual” emissions with offsets or direct removals. In Cape Town's case these were estimated at 18.8% of total BASIC emissions in 2050.

Alignment with national targets: Recent amendments to South Africa's 1st Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) have moved away from specific commitments to a 2050 target but affirm the intention to support carbon neutrality with a pathway of “just and equitable” burden sharing. Given uncertainties, on balance the City of Cape Town voluntary target can be said to be “as ambitious” as the NDC.

Conditional components: While the emissions trajectory of the City is on track for the target, several factors relating to national policy and governance, and market trends, will determine whether city-wide targets will be met. Due to national legislation, the City does not have full control over some required key intervention areas. Several amendments to the national Electricity Regulations over recent years have opened up opportunities for the City to play a role in securing and decarbonising its energy supply. While the City has procurement processes underway to purchase electricity from decentralised and IPPs and is expanding its own modest utility scale generation assets, these processes have been challenging and have many attendant business and regulatory risks. The nature of the national power system, the many reforms notwithstanding, means a reliance on coal-intensive grid power for some time to come. A wholesale electricity market is scheduled to begin trading in April 2026 however and this should drive both greater reliability of supply and progressively cleaner electricity over time.

The rail service (and some other public transport modes) within Cape Town is managed by national state-owned entities or regional government contractors, limiting the potential for significant improvements or expansions to the services required to accelerate modal shift in transport. Proposed amendments to the National Land Transport Act may however devolve the full public transport mandate to the local government to act as a Transport Authority and concessionaire of rail. In 2023/24 the national rail utility also made considerable progress in restoring service to most lines investing in tracks, stations and rolling stock. Roughly half of the collection of solid waste within the city is handled by private companies, making the monitoring and regulation of waste diversion to landfill a challenge. Buildings are a key sector in the new action plan and there is a dedicated NZC buildings program in place. Integration of new building stock into spatial planning frameworks is also essential to make public transport work. Most building stock is however constructed by private developers and a recessionary business environment with low confidence makes regulation unpopular and political traction low at this time. 

Progress: Beyond 2030 the emissions trajectories for burden sharing schemes, like Horizon 2020, that are premised on late peaking in developing countries, require very rapid decarbonisation. For a small economy like South Africa's where it is now clear, socio-economic challenges exacerbated by climate impacts will persist well beyond 2030, meeting targets will ultimately depend on technology diffusion from faster mitigating economies and the price of those technologies and their integration. The building blocks of power system decarbonisation are however in place and electric vehicles of various technologies are slowly diffusing. Cape Town remains committed to enabling these technologies where possible under its powers and mandates.

A partir de los compromisos establecidos en la legislación, planes y programas actuales estatales, municipales, metropolitanos y las directrices de C40, la visión del PACmetro busca: “Consolidar el Área Metropolitana de Guadalajara, conformada por sus nueve municipalidades, como una metrópoli carbono neutral, resiliente e inclusiva en el año 2050, mediante la acción climática metropolitana coordinada, progresiva, innovativa, transformacional y efectiva con visión a largo plazo, y alineada con el Acuerdo de París de limitar el calentamiento global a 1.5°C.”

Considerando lo anterior, y reconociendo que los efectos adversos del cambio climático exacerban la vulnerabilidad del territorio y sus habitantes, así como el alto sentido de corresponsabilidad y compromiso del AMG, el PACmetro define cuatro compromisos específicos para alcanzar la visión de largo plazo al 2050:
- Marcar la hoja de ruta para lograr una metrópoli carbono neutral a más tardar en 2050.
- Mostrar cómo la metrópoli se adaptará y mejorará su resiliencia a los riesgos relacionados con el clima.
- Informar a la ciudadanía sobre su desarrollo y avance en su implementación, presentando los beneficios esperados y alcanzados, considerando su distribución equitativa.
- Desarrollar, robustecer y consolidar los mecanismos de gobernanza, las competencias y capacidades metropolitanas para su implementación, e identificar a las personas socias que han de sumar sus esfuerzos para acelerar el cumplimiento de las metas de mitigación y objetivos de resiliencia.

Para el cumplimiento de esta meta, es necesario llevar a cabo las acciones estimadas en el escenario extendido, pues las medidas y condiciones incluidas en la modelación de emisiones del escenario 3 o ambicioso no alcanzan la carbono neutralidad, por lo que es necesario establecer mayor ambición para reducir la brecha identificada durante los periodos de los años 2030 al 2050.

 En este sentido, la trayectoria de un cuarto escenario o extendido, presenta una trayectoria que logra sostener una reducción constante de las emisiones a partir del año 2030. 

Las emisiones residuales de este escenario son de 6.5 MtCO2e en el 2050, lo que representa una reducción de 86.1% de emisiones; esta cantidad asimismo hace evidente la necesidad o demanda potencial de certificados de compensación de captura de carbono o créditos de carbono para alcanzar la neutralidad. Cabe destacar que si consideramos las absorciones que brindan los sumideros de carbono del AMG, la cantidad a compensar sería menor.

Para el cumplimiento de esta meta, es necesario llevar a cabo las acciones estimadas en el escenario extendido, pues las medidas y condiciones incluidas en la modelación de emisiones del escenario 3 o ambicioso no alcanzan la carbono neutralidad, por lo que es necesario establecer mayor ambición para reducir la brecha identificada durante los periodos de los años 2030 al 2050.

 En este sentido, la trayectoria de un cuarto escenario o extendido, presenta una trayectoria que logra sostener una reducción constante de las emisiones a partir del año 2030. 

Las emisiones residuales de este escenario son de 6.5 MtCO2e en el 2050, lo que representa una reducción de 86.1% de emisiones; esta cantidad asimismo hace evidente la necesidad o demanda potencial de certificados de compensación de captura de carbono o créditos de carbono para alcanzar la neutralidad. Cabe destacar que si consideramos las absorciones que brindan los sumideros de carbono del AMG, la cantidad a compensar sería menor.

La meta implica constituir una ciudad Carbono Neutro en 2050, de acuerdo con los escenarios construidos es posible que se requiera la consideración de créditos de carbono. En Colombia la red de distribución se compone de la matriz energética nacional que, en cerca de un 70% corresponde a fuentes hídricas y, aproximadamente, un 28% corresponde a centrales termoeléctricas. La descarbonización de la red depende del direccionamiento de las políticas nacionales. Las políticas nacionales de comercialización, apertura, e inversión son necesarias para la renovación de la flota vehicular que se encuentra compuesta en cerca del 99% por vehículos impulsados por combustibles fósiles. Es necesaria la adopción de políticas nacionales de renovación de flota que repercutan en el ámbito local. Los sistemas de transporte público masivo en Colombia son auspiciados, mayoritariamente, por fondos del gobierno nacional, su convergencia en medidas que permitan ampliar la cobertura y calidad de los gobiernos locales es un imperativo. La gestión de servicios públicos domiciliarios, incluido la recolección, aseo y separación de residuos depende de la regulación e incentivos generados por el gobierno nacional para los prestadores de servicios. Dadas las características del País, los principales esfuerzos del Estado se enfocan en la reducción de emisiones por deforestación en el marco del Sector AFOLU, las metas locales no incluyen, actualmente, este sector, lo que implica un mayor esfuerzo del gobierno local por llamar la atención del Estado Central. En el mediano plazo la adopción de un enfoque de emisiones por consumo necesitará evaluar las fuentes de materiales e insumos consumidos en la jurisdicción. column39:
A meta do Município de Porto Alegre é alcançar 100% da redução das emissões líquidas em 2050. Alcançar emissões líquidas-zero requer
a neutralização das emissões residuais de gases de efeito estufa com a quantidade equivalente
de remoções de carbono. Ou seja, esta meta visa reduzir as emissões ao máximo e alcançar o
ponto em que as emissões de GEE residuais são equilibradas por remoções durante um período
específico. A meta está em consonância com o Acordo de Paris e o Compromisso Race to Zero,
assinado pela Prefeitura de Porto Alegre. Para definir os percentuais foram consideradas ações
de mitigação que contemplam as principais fontes identificadas no inventário de emissões de GEE, como o uso de combustíveis fósseis no transporte terrestre, o consumo de energia em
fontes estacionárias e o tratamento de efluentes. É importante destacar que o inventário de emissões de Porto Alegre inclui emissões dos combustíveis utilizados pelas aeronaves que chegam e partem do aeroporto da cidade, os quais são de responsabilidade direta da companhia aérea e sob as quais a cidade não possui gerencia. Conforme as emissões residuais do Cenário Ambicioso, a maior emissão remanescente é justamente do transporte aéreo. As emissões do transporte terrestre também apresentam maior significância, especialmente devido ao consumo de diesel e gasolina no transporte particular, que representam 95% das residuais deste setor. Já as emissões remanescentes de energia estacionária são em sua maior parte por consumo de energia elétrica, mas incluem também o gás natural. Por fim, o setor de resíduos ainda apresenta algumas
emissões remanescentes devido às estações que tratam de forma anaeróbia os efluentes. As emissões remanescentes poderão ser neutralizadas por mecanismos de compensação que contribuam para remoção e, consequentemente, para o atingimento da meta
de emissões líquidas zero em 2050. Isso é possível de diferentes formas, mas uma delas é a
ampliação de projetos florestais dentro e fora do Município, com ações já direcionadas no PLAC
e novas que possam ser desenvolvidas ao longo da sua implementação.

Para estimar as emissões abrangidas pela meta no ano em que a meta foi estabelecida foi utilizada uma ferramenta, desenvolvida no software Microsoft Excel pela empresa I Care em parceria com o WRI, para a construção de um Cenário de redução de emissões baseado no crescimento populacional, econômico e regressão linear de tendências históricas de atividades. O ano base adotado como referência para a construção dos cenários foi 2016, por ser o ano do primeiro inventário de emissões elaborado por Campinas e servir de ponto de partida para acompanhar a progressão das emissões e revisão das metas de redução. Os horizontes escolhidos para as projeções foram: 2025, 2030, 2040 e 2050 e os setores considerados foram os de Energia Estacionária, Transportes e Resíduos. A meta da cidade é menos ambiciosa (em valor absoluto) do que a NDC nacional devido ao fato de que a cidade de Campinas se configura como uma área urbana já consolidada onde o range de redução das emissões de GEE é notadamente mais restrito que o nacional. Ainda, informamos que o estabelecimentos das metas de redução seguiram a faixa de redução de emissões sugerida pelo Guia de Metas Baseadas na Ciência (SBT). Considerando a emissão de GEE per capita de Campinas de 2,91 tCO2e per capita e PIB per capita de R$ 59.634,21 (US$ 11.063,86 - cotação 2021), de acordo com a
Metodologia DeadLine 2020 (C40) e o enquadramento em tipologia de cidades (emissão GEE < 5,1tCO2e per capita e PIB < US$
15 mil per capita), Campinas foi enquadrada como Baixo nos dois critérios, o que confere um perfil semelhante a cidades como
Quito, Buenos Aires e Johanesburgo, nos quais a meta indicativa de redução para 2030 é de 0 a 5% e Zero Emissões até 2050.

column39: Climate Neutrality Target by 2050 is conditioned by national policies, in particular the National Climate Neutrality Roadmap (https://descarbonizar2050.apambiente.pt/en/)\nAbout Lisbon Climate Neutrality Target:The CAP Lisbon 2030 reinforces the GHG reduction target for 2030 (Target 1; mid-term) , accelerating the path to neutrality (Target 2; long-term neutrality), aiming to reduce (in 2050) total emissions induced by the city (territorial and non-territorial) by 85% to 90%, which will require - in addition to substantial reductions - the development of strategies for managing residual emissions (estimated at 408 to 612 ktCO2e in 2050). The city of Lisbon identifies 3 possible strategies for residual emissions management:1. Emissions Removals, including possible implementation of capture, storage and/use projects (CCS/CCU) makes it possible to account for negative emissions (removals). 2. Sinks, Lisbon municipality began developing, in partnership with universities and research centers, work to quantify carbon sinks in the city (Tree cover / Meadows / Monsanto Forest Park / Green Zones / Tagus Estuary ).3. Emissions compensation is not a risk-free strategy, and if the city moves towards a compensation policy it must necessarily guarantee guiding principles of Effectiveness, Measurability, Additionality, Permanence and Absence of double counting. Taking into account the importance of the forest in Portugal and the planned creation of the Voluntary Carbon Market in Portugal, emissions offsetting will be a strategy to be taken into consideration. It is also necessary to assess whether the city will be a buyer of credits, an investor or whether it will develop its own projects (depending on factors such as time horizon, geographic origin of projects, associated costs).

2　2050年度目標及び2030年度目標の評価
本市では、下記のとおり、⑴長期的ネットゼロ目標と、⑵地球温暖化を1.5℃に抑えるための公正な分担に整合した中期的目標の二つを設定しています。

⑴ 長期的ネットゼロ目標：2050年度ネットゼロ目標のため、SBT理論に適合
⑵ 中期的目標：2030年度の区域排出量目標　5,370,000t-CO2
⑶ 中期的目標の評価 ：下記イ＞ウより、SBT理論に適合
　ア 2030年度の一人当たり目標排出量(C40平均目標)：2.9 t-CO2/人※
　　※ 出典：C40『Deadline 2020』レポート
　イ 2030年度における、Deadline2020算定排出量
　　・2030年度の札幌市の人口予測データ：1,941,000人
　　・2030年度排出総量：2.9t-CO2/人×1,941,000人=5,628,900t-CO2
　ウ 2030年度における、札幌市の排出量目標値=5,370,000t-CO2

※札幌市の温室効果ガス排出量の算定についての補足
札幌市気候変動対策行動計画に基づいて実施した主な取組の進捗状況や、札幌市から排出される温室効果ガス排出量などを把握し、毎年度公表しています。
温室効果ガス排出量の推計には国などで行っている様々な統計値を使用するため、最新値が当該年度の前々年度となります。また、統計値は修正することがあるため、最新値は速報値として取り扱っています。2年後に再度推計を行い、確定値としています。
最新のインベントリは、2022年度の速報値を採用しています。

Ottawa's population has been steadily growing since 2012, yet per capita community 
emissions are about 19 per cent lower in 2024 than in 2012. In simple terms, this means 
that even as the city added thousands of new residents, homes, and jobs, each 
person's share of emissions is significantly less than in 2012. In 2024, Ottawa's total 
community GHG emissions were roughly 5 per cent (≈ 343,000 tCO2e) lower than the 
2012 baseline. Ottawa's progress for total emissions is not unique within the national 
picture. Comparing community emissions between 2012 and 2022 demonstrates 
Toronto's community emissions are about 5 per cent below 2012 levels, Vancouver's 
have increased by approximately 9 per cent since 2012, and Calgary shows almost a 10 
per cent decrease since 2012 (driven in part by phasing out coal for electricity 
generation)1. Consistent with recent research showing many municipalities are not on 
track, Ottawa is not expected to achieve the 2025 target of a 43 per cent emissions 
reduction. Further, advancing significant emissions reductions in the community will 
require coordinated action across all sectors, as municipal levers alone, such as land 
use policy, incentives, and advocacy, while important to advance, are not sufficient.

The City of Ottawa's target is set post-coal-phase out from the grid which makes the subsequent targets even more ambitious.

 Transportation is the largest source of emissions, representing 44 per cent of 
community emissions and sitting about 5 per cent above 2012; emissions 
associated with on-road transportation account for almost 33 per cent of total 
community emissions.

• Buildings are the second largest source at 41 per cent, with an almost 16 per 
cent reduction in emissions compared to 2012. Natural gas contributes about 31 
per cent of total community emissions, and electricity about 7.5 per cent.
• Waste contributes 12 per cent and is up about 5.5 per cent since 2012; public 
and private landfills generate nearly 95 per cent of waste emissions.
• Agriculture remains a small share at about 3 per cent, which is roughly 2 per cent 
lower than in 2012.

column39: By joining the Covenant of Mayors in 2011 Sofia Municipality set a goal for GHG emission reduction with 22% in 2020. In 2018, 18.2 % has been achieved. In November 2018 Sofia Municipality has set its commitment under the Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy as follows:(1) To reduce CO2 (and possibly other greenhouse gas) emissions on its territory by at least 40% by 2030, namely through improved energy efficiency and greater use of renewable energy sources; and (2) To increase its resilience by adapting to the impacts of climate change.In order to translate these commitments into action, Sofia Municipality has undertaken the following step-by-step approach:(1) Carrying out a Baseline Emissions Inventory and a Climate Change Risk and Vulnerability Assessment;(2) Submitting a Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan within two years; and (3) Report progress at least every second year following the submission of the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan for evaluation, monitoring, and verification purposes. At the national level, Bulgaria has a joint committee within the EU. The EU and its Member States are committed to a binding target of at least 40% domestic reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared to 1990, to be fulfilled jointly. The target represents a significant progression beyond its current undertaking of a 20% emission reduction commitment by 2020 compared to 1990 (which includes the use of offsets). It is in line with the EU objective, in the context of necessary reductions according to the IPCC by developed countries as a group, to reduce its emissions by 80-95% by 2050 compared to 1990. Furthermore, it is consistent with the need for at least halving global emissions by 2050 compared to 1990. The EU and its Member States have already reduced their emissions by around 19% on 1990 levels while GDP has grown by more than 44% over the same period. As a result, average per capita emissions across the EU and its Member States have fallen from 12 tonnes CO2-eq. in 1990 to 9 tonnes CO2-eq. in 2012 and are projected to fall to around 6 tonnes CO2-eq. in 2030. The emissions in the EU and its Member States peaked in 1979. In addition, in 2020, Sofia Municipality accounted for 24,7% reduction of the emissions that is a good step to the fulfilment of even a more ambitious target like the new target set by the EU - 55% reduction until 2030.

For the baseline GHG emissions inventory and reduction target, the City of Ljubljana used a holistic approach by integrating multiple methodologies: the Global Protocol for Community-Scale Greenhouse Gas Inventories (GPC) methodology, the Covenant of Mayors (CoM) methodology, and the OPCC methodology. Each methodology played a distinct role—GPC for establishing a consistent emissions inventory, CoM for aligning with international climate commitments, and the OPCC methodology for assessing alignment with a science-based targets. This comprehensive approach was validated and further refined through ad-hoc analyses to ensure accuracy and transparency, ultimately providing a detailed and robust emissions inventory that accounts for emissions across all relevant sectors and levels.

The emissions intensity target was set considering the initial emissions and the goal of achieving net zero.

The city's plans for achieving the target are documented in the Climate City Contract (CCC), which also includes the target of reducing GHG emissions by at least 80% by 2030 compared to 2018 levels, leaving residual emissions of less than 20%.

The plan to achieve the target involves substantial investments, approximately EUR 7.8 billion, leveraging public, private, EU, and national/regional funding. column39: 수원시는 2025년, 제1차 탄소중립 녹색성장 기본계획을 수립하고, 2018년 기준연도 배출량(6,379,824 tCO2eq) 대비 40%를 감축을 2030년도 목표로 설정하였다. 이를 위해 [감축부문]에서 20개 전략 88개 단위사업을 편성하였다. 구체적으로는 건물 부문에서 6개 전략, 32개 단위사업, 수송 부문에서 4개 전략, 26개 단위사업을 편성하였고, 농축산 부문에서 1개 전략, 3개 단위사업, 자원순환(폐기물) 부문에서 3개 전략, 12개 단위사업을 편성하고 흡수원 부문에서는 3개 전략, 6개 단위사업을 편성하였다. 또한 정성사업으로만 구성된 녹색생활 및 정책 부문(기타 부문)에서는 3개 전략, 9개 단위사업을 편성하였다. 이들 단위사업은 21개 부서(과)에서 추진 중으로 기후위기 대응을 위한 온실가스 감축에 긍정적인 영향을 줄 것으로 예측된다. 한편, [기후위기 대응기반 강화 부문]은 기후위기 적응대책, 공유재산에 미치는 영향 및 대응방안, 국제 협력 및 지자체 간 협력, 교육·소통, 녹색성장 촉진, 청정에너지 전환 촉진, 정의로운 전환, 탄소중립 녹색성장 인력 양성으로 구성되었다. 장래인구추계에 의해서 2030년 수원시 인구는 1,280,120명으로 예측된다. 2025년(올해)는 기본계획의 수립 연도로, 연말에 온실가스 감축을 위한 단위사업에 대한 이행점검을 진행, 다음연도 초에 결과를 작성 후, 2026년 상반기 내로 수원시 탄소중립 녹색성장위원회의 심의를 통해 국가에 보고할 계획이다. 기본계획의 목표연도 배출량 예측 방법 등은 11번 항목의 제1차 수원시 녹색성장 기본계획 보고서의 3장 2절을 참고 바람.

Refer Chapter 6 on Scenario Planning for Future Emissions Reduction (page no. 173 to 185) and Chapter 7 on Ahmedabad's Goals and Strategies for Climate Resilience (page no. 187 to 311) of Ahmedabad Climate Resilient City Action Plan - Towards A Net Zero Future by 2070. This action plan identifies GHG mitigation targets for 2030 (short term targets), 2050 (intermediate targets) and 2070 (Net Zero Target).

Ahmedabad's Net Zero CRCAP aims to make the city climate-resilient and advance towards net zero emissions by 2070. It proposes strategies such as promoting energy efficiency in buildings, increasing RE use, adopting sustainable waste management practices, and encouraging low-carbon transport options. Ahmedabad's Climate Resilient City Action Plan (CRCAP) - Towards Net Zero by 2070 has been developed using ICLEI's Net Zero ClimateResilientCITIES methodology. This includes guidance for baseline analyses and identification, and prioritization of climate resilient strategies and targets.

Scenario Planning, a critical step in the process of developing an ambitious climate action plan, establishes the business as usual (BAU) future emissions trajectory. Emissions reduction strategies, scales of action and multiple targets are defined and analysed to arrive at two distinct emissions reduction pathways; the Progressive Action Scenario and the Net Zero Emissions Pathway.

BAU Projection: The BAU projection shows the level of GHG emissions that would result in the future if the current levels and patterns of climate action are followed. It assumes that no additional emissions reduction efforts and measures will be undertaken, beyond those already in place. The BAU projection represents the 'baseline condition' and serves as a reference point for assessing the impact of emissions reduction scenarios or pathways.

Progressive Action Scenario: The Progressive Action scenario represents the level of GHG emissions resulting from increased levels of climate action being implemented at the city-scale as compared to the BAU scenario. It considers the goals and guidelines of national and state government policies and programs, while being defined by and reflective of on-ground scenarios. Factors such as local conditions, current urban infrastructure and service provision, level of adoption of climate solutions, resources, and capacities are considered while determining the targets and actions proposed.

Net Zero Pathway: The Net Zero Pathway is based on the commitment of Government of India to achieve net zero emissions by 2070. It is defined by ambitious climate actions and efforts that are required for the city to transition towards meeting net zero GHG targets by 2070. The actions in this pathway build on the targets set by the national and state government through various plans, policies, and programs to realize this goal.

Guiding Principles for estimating the BAU scenario:
1. The relationship between the quantum of emissions and the rate of urbanization is assumed to be directly proportional. 
2. Urbanization rate is influenced by the population and economic growth, which are affected by interdependent factors such as secondary and tertiary sector growth, education levels, birth and death rates, life expectancy, and migration.
3. Urbanization refers to expanding urban centres in terms of geographical area and population, driven by shifts in the economy from primary to secondary, tertiary, or quaternary activities.

For modelling of the projected BAU emissions, three different urbanization pathways have been evaluated based on the UN's World Urbanisation Prospects methodologies, the IPCC-endorsed Shared Socio-economic Pathways, and guidance from the Global Cities Institute.
