column39: 屏東縣政府以2020年500.8萬噸CO2e排放量作為基準，以2030年減碳30%、2040年減碳65%及2050年實現碳排歸零作為目標前進，其中雖本縣2030年初步減碳目標為30%，然依據本縣主要減碳項目如再生能源設置量、綠建築推動、綠色產業轉型、綠色運輸發展及提升資源回收量等，至2030年可減碳約226萬噸左右，搭配推動有機農業、提升造林面積等方式增加碳匯量，預計可於2030年提前達成250萬噸(50%)之減碳目標量，以下針對各項主要減碳項目進行說明。<建築>2030年前要求新建築及公有建築完成能效盤查、揭露及管制，並完成公有建築85%取得近零建築標章之目標，預計可減碳約24萬噸CO2e。<產業>*推估2030年前鍋爐全面燃氣化，可減少3萬噸排放，而事業單位實際推動每年節能1%，可減少15萬噸排放，總減碳量約18萬噸左右。*2030年、2040年及2050年累計完成82家(30%)、136家(50%)及191家(70%)企業碳盤查。為協助其有效降低碳排放，本縣將針對名單中排放量前50%之單位，預計於2030、2040及2050年累計完成41家次、70家次及100家次節能輔導作業。2030、2040及2050年達成25家次、40家次及60家次企業實施「PAS 2060 碳中和」並取得零碳認證。*本縣契約容量5000 kW以上用電大戶，於2030年前需建置10%綠電、儲能裝置、購買再生能源憑證或繳納代金(四擇一)*導入最新廢水處理規劃設計技術，藉由製程回用調整、廢水回收再利用來提升水資源使用效率，預計於2030達成6萬CMD(m3/day)，以BOD約90%去除率換算其減碳量，於2030年可減少14萬公噸CO2e左右。*目前電動曳引車與電動重型機具普遍存在續行較短問題，考量實際使用需計算工作時數與距離，以小範圍區域作為示範點，輔導業者汰換燃油工作載具，如2030年前工業區及科技園區工作載具全面電動(氣)化。<交通>*於2030年完成89,471台(30%)電動汽車汰換量，及185,688台(30%)電動機車汰換量，預計可減碳30萬噸CO2e。*於2030年達到公務車及市區公車100%使用電動車。*於2030年完成汽車充電站設置量2,000座(含200座快充站)之目標。*以2030 Youbike累計租借人次達到600萬為目標。<再生能源>*2030年目標將綠能設置量提升至2GW，預計可減碳115萬噸CO2e。<廢棄物>為降低廢棄物產生之溫室氣體排放量，本府積極鼓勵民眾落實資源回收，鼓勵民種綠色消費、源頭減量、資源回收、再使用及再生利用等，預計於2030年達成65%資源回收率、以每公斤廢棄物燃燒排碳量約為0.757公斤CO2e計算，至2030年約可減碳10萬公噸CO2e左右。另外有鑑於本縣作為農業大縣，為減少本縣在農業廢棄物方面所造成之溫室氣體排放，因此本府打造一條龍農業廢棄物妥善處理體系，協助農民處理農業廢棄物、覆土膠布及相關資材等，預計至2030年可減碳約15萬噸左右。The Pingtung County Government took 2020 (5,008,000 tons of greenhouse gas emission) as base line and aims to reduce 30% of greenhouse gas emission in 2030, 65% in 2040, and achieve net zero emissions in 2050. Although the County's initial target in 2030 is to reduce 30% of greenhouse gas emission, the County can reduce more than 30% according to the county's major carbon reduction projects, such as increasing renewable energy capacity, green building, green industry, green transportation, and recycling, etc.By 2030, Pingtung County can reduce about 2.26 million tons of greenhouse gas emission. It is estimated that the carbon reduction target of 2.5 million tons (50% of greenhouse gas emission) can be achieved ahead of schedule in 2030 by promoting organic agriculture and increasing afforestation area to increase carbon sinks.The following describes the main projects to reduce greenhouse gas emission:<Buildings>New buildings and public buildings should finish carbon inventory, disclosure and control. 85% of public buildings should obtain near zero building certificates. It is estimated that these strategies can reduce 240,000 tons of CO2e.<Industry>*Coal-fired boilers will be fully replaced by gas-fired by 2030, which can reduce 30,000 tons of GHG emissions every year. Enterprises are asked to have 1% of annual energy saving, which can reduce 150,000 tons of GHG emissions every year. With the strategies mentioned above, it is estimated to reduce 180,000 tons of greenhouse gas emission in total.*30% of enterprises in Pingtung County should complete their GHG Inventory by 2030, and emission ranked No.1 ~ 50 should have energy saving counseling. 10% of enterprises should get carbon neutral certificates by 2030.*By 2030, electricity consumers with a contracted capacity of 5,000 kW or more in Pingtung County are required to install 10% of green energy, energy storage devices, purchasing renewable energy certificates or fined (one out of four).*It is estimated to reach 60,000 CMD(m3/day) in 2030 by reusing waste water after proper treatments. It is estimated to reduce 140,000 tons of CO2e in 2030.*At present, electric heavy-duty equipment or vehicles generally have the problem of short operating endurance. Considering the actual use, it is necessary to calculate the working hours and distance and replace fossil fuel equipment or vehicles with electric ones in industrial zones of high-technology parks.<Transportation>*It is estimated to reach 30% electric cars (89,471 cars) and electric two-wheel vehicles (185,688 motorcycles) in 2030. It is estimated to reduce 300,000 tons of CO2e in 2030.*Official vehicles will be 100% electric cars by 2030.*Buses will be 100% electric buses by 2030.*There will be 2000 charging piles, including 200 fast charging stations, by 2030. *Public bike users are estimated to reach 6,000,000 people by 2030.<Renewable energy>*Installed capacity of renewable energy is estimated to reach 2GW in 2030. It is estimated to reduce 1150,000 tons of CO2e in 2030.<Waste>In order to reduce the greenhouse gas emissions caused by waste, Pingtung County Government actively encourages green consumption, reusing and recycling, etc. It is expected to achieve 65% of recycling rate in 2030, reducing 100,000 tons of greenhouse gas emission based on carbon footprint of incineration which is 0.757 kg CO2e/kg.In addition, Pingtung County Government also helps farmers to deal with the agricultural waste by set up one-stop agricultural waste disposal centers to assist farmers in handling plastic films, tapes, and related agricultural waste. It is estimated that it can reduce about 150,000 tons of greenhouse gas emission by 2030.

First, it is expected to make 85% of old buildings have the near-zero building mark in 2030, which can save about 730 million kWh of electricity and reduce 370,000 tons of CO2e.In 2040, Pingtung County will make 100% of old buildings become net-zero buildings, which can save about 830 million kWh of electricity and reduce 420,000 tons of CO2e. Moreover, Pingtung County will also promote the installation of solar photovoltaic panels on the roof of buildings, and 20% of electricity will be supplied by renewable energy, which will reduce 160,000 tons of CO2e.In 2050, Pingtung County estimates to achieve 100% net-zero buildings, which are expected to save 1.66 billion kWh of electricity and reduce 800,000 tons of CO2e.<Industry> replacing high-pollution boilers, integrating regional energy resources, and installing smart energy management systemsBy 2030, the full gasification of boilers can reduce 30,000 tons of emissions. Vijayawada Net-zero CRCAP charts a pathway to net‑zero emissions by 2047, using scenario planning to set short‑term (2030), intermediate (2040), and long‑term (2047) mitigation targets and to compare a Business‑as‑Usual baseline with two pathways: a Progressive Action Scenario and a Net Zero Pathway aligned with India's 2070 commitment and Andhra Pradesh state's Swarna Andhra Vision of 2047. The plan prioritizes energy‑efficient buildings, expanded renewable energy, sustainable waste and water management, and low‑carbon mobility, developed through ICLEI's Net Zero ClimateResilientCITIES methodology, which guides baseline assessment, strategy prioritization, and target‑setting. The BAU trajectory reflects future emissions if no additional measures are taken beyond current policies, while the Progressive Action Scenario scales city‑level actions consistent with national and state guidance and grounded in local conditions, infrastructure, adoption levels, resources, and capacity. The Net Zero Pathway adds more ambitious measures to close the gap to net zero by 2047, building on higher‑order policy targets and requiring deeper shifts in technology, behavior, and systems. BAU estimation follows principles that link emissions to urbanization rates driven by demographic and economic dynamics, and evaluates rapid, moderate, and slow urbanization pathways (per UN urbanization prospects, IPCC‑endorsed SSPs, and Global Cities Institute guidance); Vijayawada's Net-zero CRCAP adopts the moderate urbanization scenario based on the comparison and analysis of its historic and future population growth. Implementation will be tracked through key performance indicators; see the Monitoring & Tracking Progress section for details on metrics and governance for transparent progress review.

Beşiktaş Municipality has set ambitious targets within the framework of its Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP, 2024) to significantly reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and transition toward a more sustainable energy system. The central target involves achieving a 41,6% reduction in emissions by 2030 compared to the Business-as-Usual (BAU) projection, reducing community-wide emissions from an expected 1206234 tCO₂e (BAU in 2030) to 704701 tCO₂e. This target is based on a 2022 baseline of 995368 tCO₂e and was established in line with the Covenant of Mayors framework and the Paris Agreement (2015).

To achieve this, the municipality has launched multiple initiatives in energy efficiency, renewable energy integration, sustainable transportation, and waste management.

Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy Projects: Solar panel installations on public and residential buildings, energy audits in municipal facilities, and the adoption of smart energy management systems have already been initiated. These are expected to contribute significantly toward the 2030 target.

Sustainable Transportation: Expansion of the municipal electric vehicle (EV) fleet and installation of EV charging stations are directly reducing emissions from transport, one of the district's major emission sources.

Waste Management Improvements: Expanded recycling programs and organic waste treatment initiatives are reducing methane emissions and supporting a circular economy.

While progress has been moderate so far, securing adequate funding for large-scale infrastructure investments remains a challenge. The municipality is actively seeking partnerships and exploring innovative financing mechanisms to bridge this gap. Collaboration with national-level government policies on renewable energy and grid decarbonization will also be critical to success.

Beşiktaş's climate efforts not only serve the local community but also act as a model for other municipalities in Turkey and internationally. The municipality continues to monitor progress through annual GHG inventory updates and SECAP reporting.

Note on methodology: The SECAP target (704701 tCO₂e) differs from CDP's auto-calculated figure (581295 tCO₂e) because CDP applies the reduction percentage directly to the baseline year emissions, whereas the SECAP methodology defines the 41,6% reduction relative to the BAU projection for 2030. Both figures are reported for transparency.

La Municipalidad de Independencia tiene como meta reducir las emisiones de Gases de Efecto Invernadero (GEI) en al menos un 30% para el año 2030. Este compromiso busca mitigar los impactos locales del cambio climático y avanzar hacia un desarrollo más sustentable y resiliente para la comuna.

Para alcanzar este objetivo, se han definido diversas estrategias. Entre ellas se encuentra el fomento de la gestión integral de residuos orgánicos e inorgánicos, impulsando la creación de infraestructura que permita su valorización y minimice la generación de desechos. Asimismo, se busca incentivar la educación ambiental con un enfoque en la valorización de residuos, promoviendo una cultura de sostenibilidad y responsabilidad ambiental dentro de la comunidad.

Otra de las líneas de acción considera la optimización en el uso de los recursos energéticos, lo que implica reducir las emisiones de GEI asociadas a su consumo. En este marco, se proyecta la implementación de medidas de eficiencia energética (EE) y de energías renovables no convencionales (ERNC), que faciliten la generación local de energía destinada a los sectores residencial y comercial. Junto con ello, se pretende convertir a Independencia en un referente en sostenibilidad energética, fortaleciendo la educación y sensibilización de la comunidad respecto del uso responsable de los recursos energéticos y de la importancia de reducir el consumo desde la red de distribución.

De igual manera, la Municipalidad considera prioritario promover la movilidad y el desarrollo de infraestructuras sostenibles, con el propósito de mitigar los efectos del cambio climático tanto a nivel institucional como comunal. También se contempla el establecimiento de un sistema de monitoreo y registro de información ambiental que respalde la toma de decisiones basada en datos, además de medir y certificar la huella de carbono municipal y comunal, lo que permitirá evaluar con mayor precisión el impacto ambiental y diseñar estrategias efectivas de reducción.

Es relevante destacar que, según el Inventario de Emisiones 2022, las emisiones de Independencia alcanzaron las 280.362 toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente, cifra que representa una disminución respecto de las 295.165 toneladas registradas en 2020, lo que equivale a una reducción del 5%. Si bien este avance resulta positivo, es necesario redoblar los esfuerzos para cumplir la meta de reducción establecida para el año 2030.

Para alcanzar la meta de mitigación relacionada con las emisiones del sector transporte, se propone implementar el Plan de Movilidad, cuyo objetivo es fortalecer el transporte sostenible en la comuna mediante la instalación de nuevas vías y el mejoramiento de ciclovías existentes, como la de Av. Fermín Vivaceta. Este plan contempla la incorporación de señalización adecuada, incluyendo zonas 30, con el fin de aumentar la seguridad de ciclistas y peatones, incentivar el uso de medios no motorizados y reducir las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero.

Los medios de implementación asociados a esta medida corresponden a los kilómetros de ciclovías construidas, el porcentaje de veredas recuperadas, el número de puntos de scooters eléctricos habilitados y la cantidad de charlas de educación ambiental relacionadas con movilidad sostenible.

Asimismo, se propone fomentar el uso de vehículos eléctricos en aquellas labores municipales que lo requieran, priorizando proyectos que integren esta tecnología por sobre otros tipos de combustibles. En el marco de esta iniciativa, se contempla aumentar la flota de vehículos eléctricos municipales y garantizar su adecuada mantención, a fin de optimizar su eficiencia y prolongar su vida útil. El medio de implementación de esta medida corresponde al número de vehículos eléctricos adquiridos.

Respecto de la disminución de emisiones en este sector, al comparar los inventarios de 2020 y 2024 se observa una reducción del 14,87%.

Para alcanzar una reducción de emisiones en el sector energía, se propone en primer lugar promover la utilización de paneles solares fotovoltaicos en edificios municipales y viviendas. Se instalarán paneles solares en espacios públicos y privados de la comuna, fomentando así la eficiencia energética y el uso de energías renovables. Las obras contemplan el refuerzo de cubiertas, la instalación de equipos fotovoltaicos en zonas óptimas para su funcionamiento y mantenimiento, y su conexión a la red eléctrica. Los medios de verificación de esta medida corresponden al número de paneles solares implementados.

En segundo lugar, se plantea la implementación de un programa de capacitación comunitaria sobre eficiencia energética. Este programa incluirá talleres orientados a prácticas que contribuyan a la disminución del consumo energético en los hogares, la promoción de la eficiencia energética y la difusión de los diferentes tipos de energías renovables no convencionales, así como de las ecotecnias presentes en el Centro de Prácticas Ambientales. Los medios de verificación de esta medida corresponden al número de vecinos capacitados y a la cantidad de charlas impartidas.

Actualmente, al comparar los dos últimos inventarios de Gases de Efecto Invernadero evaluados (2020 y 2022), se observa un aumento de 427 toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente, lo que evidencia la necesidad de incentivar con mayor fuerza la eficiencia energética en los sectores residencial, comercial e institucional.

column39:
Para avanzar en la reducción de emisiones en el sector de residuos, la Municipalidad ha definido tres líneas de acción. La primera corresponde a un programa de capacitación orientado al sector domiciliario, privado y a establecimientos educacionales de todos los niveles, con el fin de sensibilizar sobre la correcta gestión de residuos y sus implicancias ambientales, sanitarias y sociales. Su efectividad se medirá según el número de charlas impartidas y personas capacitadas.
La segunda línea consiste en el desarrollo de un modelo comunal para la gestión de residuos orgánicos, mediante un plan integral de recolección, valorización y tratamiento en ferias libres, plazas y hogares. Este contempla la ampliación del servicio en ferias como El Pino, Colón y Las Cañas, la habilitación de puntos de entrega voluntaria en espacios comunitarios y la generación de alianzas público-privadas que aseguren una disposición sustentable en una planta con resolución sanitaria. El impacto de este plan se evaluará a partir de los kilogramos valorizados y las vermicomposteras distribuidas.
La tercera línea aborda la instalación y fortalecimiento de puntos limpios y verdes para el reciclaje de residuos inorgánicos en sectores estratégicos de la comuna. Este plan se enmarca en la jerarquía de reducción, reutilización y reciclaje, y contará con el apoyo de los Sistemas de Gestión GIRO y ReSimple, responsables de financiar su implementación en conformidad con la Ley N°20.920. De forma complementaria, se aplicará un Plan de Reciclaje Municipal en oficinas y departamentos, con indicadores asociados al volumen recolectado y a la reducción por tipo de residuo.
Dado que los residuos orgánicos representan el 52% del total generado en la comuna, se fomentarán alianzas público-privadas para su tratamiento en la planta municipal de vermicompostaje, junto con la entrega de vermicomposteras domiciliarias con asistencia técnica. Para los residuos inorgánicos domiciliarios, se habilitarán puntos móviles de recolección que permitan ampliar la cobertura del servicio.
Finalmente, los inventarios de gases de efecto invernadero muestran un incremento del 18,45% entre 2020 y 2024, explicado por 6.274 toneladas adicionales de residuos domiciliarios no valorizados y 7.481 toneladas provenientes del sector no domiciliario.

The Climate Action Plan also assumes the sustainable development of the navy weapons yard, which is currently held up due to property transfer issues from the navy to the City of Concord. Further, some of the upgrades required by the CAP in the residential and private sectors, such as the time-of-sale residential weatherization disclosure, rely on additional, voluntary actions on the part of private business owners to realize emissions reductions. 

We have made significant progress towards our target. 

1. The City approved an Environmental Purchasing Policy. The IT department purchases only energy efficient equipment with EnergyStar certifications. 
2. Achieved carbon neutrality at events through conservation, efficiency, recycling, alternative transportation, and other GHG reduction strategies. 
3. Adopting a community-wide urban forestry management plan
4. Phased out CFC containing refrigerants
5. Fleet Management Department, Parks Division, Printing Services, Civic Center are Bay Area Green Business certified by ABAG.
6. The City adopts the latest version of the CALGreen Code every three years when the latest version is published. 
7. The 2019 California Residential Code requires Net Zero Energy standards for residential development and commercial development in 2030. 
8. In 2016, the City partnered with the Rising Sun Energy Center to host youth to perform 294 residential home energy assessments in Concord, leading to installation of energy and water saving devices that reduced greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to removing three residential properties' electricity use for one year. This program is anticipated in Summer 2025 as well. 
9. The City has authorized five PACE providers providing financing energy and water efficient upgrades which are promoted and identified on the City's Webpage and has included brochures from PACE providers at the Permit Center. 
10. The County provides outreach to Concord residents promoting participation in the building energy rating system. Since 2019, at least 728 homes have been scored for efficiency through the Home Energy Score. BayREN provides information to County residents and businesses about energy efficiency and all-electric buildings. 11. The City's ESCO contract completed the replacement of HVAC at City Buildings, installed a 191 kW photovoltaic system for the pool to reduce energy used by the circulation pump, installed solar at the Concord Community Park, and replaced some lighting.
12. City installed occupancy sensors shutting down AC and lighting in unoccupied rooms.
13. PG&E conducted an Automated Demand Response assessment of the City's facilities, resulting in many identifications defaulting to Peak Day Pricing. 
14. The Planning Division began working on an outreach program on efficient appliances and energy rebates and incentives in January 2025. 
The City provides links to local, state, and federal incentive programs for efficient appliances, home energy upgrades, and EVs. 
15. The City implemented instant solar PV permitting using SolarAPP.
16. The City has replaced induction lamp technology in streetlights. As of June 2024, 35% of 10,677 streetlights citywide have been converted to LED, and the remaining 65% is expected to occur by the end of 2025. Public Works has also completed the completed the removal of 257 old fluorescent ceiling lamps with LED MCP07 Canopy fixtures with PIR sensors in the Municipal Garage. 
17. The Planning Department references construction mitigation measures from the Bay Area Air Quality Management Department's air quality guidelines. 
18. State legislative changes, including AB 341, AB 1826, and SB 1383 influenced the diversion of solid waste from landfills. Mount Diablo Resource Recovery, a waste and recycling company, supports this effort by sharing information and resources through newsletters, billing inserts, and distributing outreach materials, as well as providing technical assistance to schools, businesses, and community groups. 
19. The Bicycle, Pedestrian, & Safe Routes to Transit Plan was adopted in September 2016. The Plan includes vision, goals, objectives, policies, programs and projects with cost estimates, and infrastructure design guidelines. 
20. The City's fleet has been reduced by at least 10% as per the CAP goal, and the City continues to evaluate vehicle need every two years as a part of the budget process. This includes considering hybrid and EVs where applicable. 
21. Police and Public Works have implemented a vehicle management system called EcoLock to significantly lessen, but not completely eliminate, idling vehicles.
22. City employees are allowed to telecommute up to three days per week.

column39: On November 3, 2009, the City Council adopted voluntary greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction targets for the community with initial targets for 2012, 2015, 2020, and 2050. These targets set an absolute reduction in total emissions below a baseline year of 2005. The targets were developed and adopted in response to the Global Warming Solutions Act of 2006 (Assembly Bill 32), which requires California to reduce Statewide GHG emissions. Subsequently, through the City's Climate Protection Roadmap, the City Council adopted interim targets at five-year intervals between 2020 and 2050 to track the City's progress more closely. On December 3, 2019, Council adopted revised GHG reduction targets for the years 2025 to 2050 that decline by a constant annual percentage rather than a constant amount of metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (MT CO2e) each year. All of Mountain View's GHG inventories have been prepared using a national standard developed by the ICLEI—Local Governments for Sustainability (formerly International Council for Local Environmental Initiatives). This standard, the U.S. Community Protocol for Accounting and Reporting of Greenhouse Gas Emissions (the Protocol), establishes reporting requirements and accounting guidance for quantifying GHG emissions. Staff used the Protocol to examine emissions in five sectors: energy use, transportation (on-road vehicles), waste, water (potable water use and wastewater treatment), and off-road mobile sources (construction and commercial/industrial equipment).

column39: On April 12, 2020, the City Council passed a resolution for Mountain View to become a carbon-neutral city by 2045. To achieve carbon neutrality, this would mean that in addition to achieving the adopted 2045 GHG reduction target of 75% below 2005 levels, Mountain View would balance any remaining GHG emissions with carbon sequestration projects (such as planting trees or restoring wetlands) or carbon offsets. Following a referral from Council to the Council Sustainability Committee (CSC), at CSC meetings on April 19, 2022 and June 22, 2022, staff presented the implications for accelerating Mountain View's adopted carbon-neutrality target year. The CSC approved the proposed hybrid approach, which would entail completing targeted analysis to develop a road map for carbon neutrality by 2035, exploring opportunities to build partnerships and leverage private financing, and developing an approach to address residual emissions that remain after the carbon-neutrality target year. As part of the discussion, staff recommended that the City focus on the decarbonization of buildings and transportation by 2035 as the primary strategy toward achieving accelerated carbon neutrality.

column39: Refer Chapter 7 on Scenario Planning for Future Emissions Reduction (page no. 135 to 154) and Chapter 8 on Kakinada's Goals and Strategies for Climate Resilience (page no. 155 to 247) of Kakinada Net-zero Climate Resilient City Action Plan (CRCAP). Kakinada Net-zero CRCAP charts a pathway to net‑zero emissions by 2047, using scenario planning to set short‑term (2030), intermediate (2040), and long‑term (2047) mitigation targets and to compare a Business‑as‑Usual baseline with two pathways: a Progressive Action Scenario and a Net Zero Pathway aligned with India's 2070 commitment and Andhra Pradesh state's Swarna Andhra Vision of 2047. The plan prioritizes energy‑efficient buildings, expanded renewable energy, sustainable waste and water management, and low‑carbon mobility, developed through ICLEI's Net Zero ClimateResilientCITIES methodology, which guides baseline assessment, strategy prioritization, and target‑setting. The BAU trajectory reflects future emissions if no additional measures are taken beyond current policies, while the Progressive Action Scenario scales city‑level actions consistent with national and state guidance and grounded in local conditions, infrastructure, adoption levels, resources, and capacity. The Net Zero Pathway adds more ambitious measures to close the gap to net zero by 2047, building on higher‑order policy targets and requiring deeper shifts in technology, behavior, and systems. BAU estimation follows principles that link emissions to urbanization rates driven by demographic and economic dynamics, and evaluates rapid, moderate, and slow urbanization pathways (per UN urbanization prospects, IPCC‑endorsed SSPs, and Global Cities Institute guidance); Kakinada's Net-zero CRCAP adopts the moderate urbanization scenario based on the comparison and analysis of its historic and future population growth. Implementation will be tracked through key performance indicators; see the Monitoring & Tracking Progress section for details on metrics and governance for transparent progress review.

Kakinada Net-zero CRCAP charts a pathway to net‑zero emissions by 2047, using scenario planning to set short‑term (2030), intermediate (2040), and long‑term (2047) mitigation targets and to compare a Business‑as‑Usual baseline with two pathways: a Progressive Action Scenario and a Net Zero Pathway aligned with India's 2070 commitment and Andhra Pradesh state's Swarna Andhra Vision of 2047. The plan prioritizes energy‑efficient buildings, expanded renewable energy, sustainable waste and water management, and low‑carbon mobility, developed through ICLEI's Net Zero ClimateResilientCITIES methodology, which guides baseline assessment, strategy prioritization, and target‑setting. The BAU trajectory reflects future emissions if no additional measures are taken beyond current policies, while the Progressive Action Scenario scales city‑level actions consistent with national and state guidance and grounded in local conditions, infrastructure, adoption levels, resources, and capacity. The Net Zero Pathway adds more ambitious measures to close the gap to net zero by 2047, building on higher‑order policy targets and requiring deeper shifts in technology, behavior, and systems. BAU estimation follows principles that link emissions to urbanization rates driven by demographic and economic dynamics, and evaluates rapid, moderate, and slow urbanization pathways (per UN urbanization prospects, IPCC‑endorsed SSPs, and Global Cities Institute guidance); Kakinada's Net-zero CRCAP adopts the moderate urbanization scenario based on the comparison and analysis of its historic and future population growth. Implementation will be tracked through key performance indicators; see the Monitoring & Tracking Progress section for details on metrics and governance for transparent progress review.

The target was adopted for implementation as part of the Climate Contract, which was submitted to the European Commission at the end of 2024 and received a Mission Label in 2025. The city of Rzeszów aims to reduce GHG emissions by 80,06% by 2030 compared to the base year of 2022.
It should be noted that due to the lack of precise data, the reduction that could result from the project involving the development and modernization of the city's electricity infrastructure has not been estimated. However, considering the development plans of the companies responsible for the electricity and gas networks, which are very ambitious and include actions consistent with the goal of climate neutrality, it can be concluded that by 2030, the project will contribute to reducing CO2 emissions.
By area, CO2e reductions are as follows:
Stationary energy - 81.06% reduction from the area (839,717 tCO2e)
- Transport - 80.08% reduction from the area (275,694 tCO2e)
- Waste - 14.33% reduction from the area (2,114 tCO2e).
Considering the above, residual emissions will come from the following areas: stationary energy, transport, waste, and IPPU. It should be noted that tasks in these areas will be accelerated and intensified to maximize GHG emission reductions. Investments in green infrastructure and nature-based solutions will also be developed, which, in addition to CO2 absorption, have enormous adaptive value, crucial in a changing climate. The city is also exploring the potential for technological capture and permanent storage of CO2.

De acuerdo con lo señalado en el Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático, la meta de mitigación buscan reducir las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero y
disminuir la huella ecológica de la comuna. Basadas en las fichas de medidas, las principales
metas de mitigación para Colina son: ● Reducción del 30% de las emisiones de CO₂eq al 2035
○ Implementar energías renovables en sistemas de agua potable rural (APRs),
edificios públicos y viviendas.
○ Promover muros verdes y techos verdes en infraestructura pública y privada
para reducir el consumo energético y mejorar el microclima urbano.
○ Incentivar la movilidad sostenible mediante ciclovías, transporte público
eléctrico y senderos multipropósito.
● Valorización del 60% de los residuos orgánicos municipales al 2030
○ Implementar sistemas de compostaje y digestores comunitarios.
○ Promover la educación ambiental y la economía circular en colegios y barrio.
● Aumentar la cobertura de arbolado urbano y reforestación en un 25% para 2030 con
respecto al año base
○ Estrategia de manejo y protección del arbolado urbano y reforestación de
laderas y áreas erosionadas con especies nativas.

Dire Dawa City is committed to achieving carbon neutrality by 2050, with an 83.75% absolute reduction in emissions relative to the Business-as-Usual (BAU) trajectory. An interim milestone of a 54.5% absolute reduction below BAU by 2030 has also been set. These targets are expressed as absolute citywide reductions, rather than per capita or emissions intensity metrics, and are fully aligned with Ethiopia's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) and Climate Resilient Green Economy (CRGE) Strategy. They are underpinned by mitigation measures across the industry, transport, energy, and waste sectors.

Achievement of these targets, however, is contingent on enabling policies and financial support beyond the direct control of the city administration. Key external enablers include:

Resource mobilization and financial support from the federal government and multilateral organizations.

Establishment and enforcement of Low-Emission Zone (LEZ) regulations by the Federal Transport Authority.

Tariff reforms (Time-of-Use and Lifeline tariffs) adopted by the Ethiopian Electric Utility.

Adoption of a Green Procurement Policy by the Ministry of Finance and Economic Development.

Mandatory waste-sorting legislation enacted by the Federal EPA.

Feed-in Tariff / Net-Metering regulations implemented by the Ethiopian Electric Utility.

Review and enforcement of Construction Permit Standards to ensure energy-efficient buildings.

Revisions to the National Building Code to mandate energy efficiency and climate-resilient construction.

El Plan PUQ 30/30 es una iniciativa pionera de la Municipalidad de Punta Arenas, concebida como parte de la estrategia de mitigación del Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático (PACCC). Su objetivo central es lograr una reducción del 30% de las emisiones de Gases de Efecto Invernadero (GEI) al año 2030, en línea con las metas nacionales establecidas en la Ley Marco de Cambio Climático y con los compromisos internacionales de Chile.

Este plan se fundamenta en una alianza público-privada de cooperación climática, en la cual la Municipalidad convoca a todos los entes emisores de la comuna —incluyendo empresas, instituciones públicas, universidades, organizaciones sociales y actores comunitarios— a sumarse voluntariamente a un esfuerzo conjunto. La idea es que cada actor pueda comprometerse con medidas de reducción de emisiones en sus propias operaciones y aportar, al mismo tiempo, al cumplimiento de la meta comunal. 
El PUQ 30/30 se concibe, además, como un espacio innovador de gobernanza climática local, ya que trasciende la acción municipal e invita a la corresponsabilidad. De esta forma, se fortalece la relación con la comunidad y con los sectores productivos, consolidando a Punta Arenas como una comuna comprometida con la acción climática y con la transición justa hacia un modelo más sostenible.

Al ser el primer plan comunal de mitigación con metas cuantificables, PUQ 30/30 se proyecta como un hito estratégico: marca la hoja de ruta hacia la descarbonización local y alinea a la comuna con las políticas regionales y nacionales en materia de cambio climático.

column39: La révision du PCAET a été lancée en 2023 et la nouvelle stratégie climat-air-énergie, qui vise la neutralité carbone à 2050, a été validée en conseil métropolitain en mars 2025.\nAvec l'hypothèse de la préservation et du renforce-ment du puits de carbone naturel du territoire métropolitain, l'atteinte de la neutralité carbone à l'horizon 2050 suppose une réduction des émissions de GES de -97% par rapport à 2005 (4 885 kteqCO2/an en 2005). A court terme, la Métropole s'engage à renforcer les actions pour atteindre d'ici 2030 une réduction de -71% des émissions de GES par rapport à 2005, soit une réduction de 41% par rapport à 2021. Cette réduction sera rendue possible notamment par le programme d'actions AEC 2027-2032 et la mobilisation de toutes les parties pre-nantes du territoire, qui seront formalisées dans \'l'Accord de Rouen pour le Climat #2\'. Néanmoins le secteur industriel reste un secteur \'externe\' aux compétences métropolitaines et qu'il faudra fortement mobiliser viser une décarbonation très importante.\nIl conviendra d'agir dans tous les secteurs : indus-trie, résidentiel, tertiaire, transport routier et non routier, déchets, et dans une moindre mesure agri-culture.

column39: Refer Chapter 7 on Scenario Planning for Future Emissions Reduction and Chapter 8 on Vadodara's Goals and Strategies for Climate Resilience of Vadodara Climate Resilient City Action Plan - Towards A Net Zero Future by 2070. This action plan identifies GHG mitigation targets for 2030 (short term targets), 2050 (intermediate targets) and 2070 (Net Zero Target). Vadodara's Net Zero CRCAP aims to make the city climate-resilient and advance towards net zero emissions by 2070. It proposes strategies such as promoting energy efficiency in buildings, increasing RE use, adopting sustainable waste management practices, and encouraging low-carbon transport options. Vadodara's Climate Resilient City Action Plan (CRCAP) - Towards Net Zero by 2070 has been developed using ICLEI's Net Zero ClimateResilientCITIES methodology. This includes guidance for baseline analyses and identification, and prioritization of climate resilient strategies and targets. Scenario Planning, a critical step in the process of developing an ambitious climate action plan, establishes the business as usual (BAU) future emissions trajectory. Emissions reduction strategies, scales of action and multiple targets are defined and analysed to arrive at two distinct emissions reduction pathways; the Progressive Action Scenario and the Net Zero Emissions Pathway. BAU Projection: The BAU projection shows the level of GHG emissions that would result in the future if the current levels and patterns of climate action are followed. It assumes that no additional emissions reduction efforts and measures will be undertaken, beyond those already in place. The BAU projection represents the 'baseline condition' and serves as a reference point for assessing the impact of emissions reduction scenarios or pathways. Progressive Action Scenario: The Progressive Action scenario represents the level of GHG emissions resulting from increased levels of climate action being implemented at the city-scale as compared to the BAU scenario. It considers the goals and guidelines of national and state government policies and programs, while being defined by and reflective of on-ground scenarios. Factors such as local conditions, current urban infrastructure and service provision, level of adoption of climate solutions, resources, and capacities are considered while determining the targets and actions proposed. Net Zero Pathway: The Net Zero Pathway is based on the commitment of Government of India to achieve net zero emissions by 2070. It is defined by ambitious climate actions and efforts that are required for the city to transition towards meeting net zero GHG targets by 2070. The actions in this pathway build on the targets set by the national and state government through various plans, policies, and programs to realize this goal. Guiding Principles for estimating the BAU scenario: 1. The relationship between the quantum of emissions and the rate of urbanization is assumed to be directly proportional. 2. Urbanization rate is influenced by the population and economic growth, which are affected by interdependent factors such as secondary and tertiary sector growth, education levels, birth and death rates, life expectancy, and migration. 3. Urbanization refers to expanding urban centres in terms of geographical area and population, driven by shifts in the economy from primary to secondary, tertiary, or quaternary activities. 4. For modelling of the projected BAU emissions, three different urbanization pathways have been evaluated based on the UN's World Urbanisation Prospects methodologies, the IPCC-endorsed Shared Socio-economic Pathways, and guidance from the Global Cities Institute. These pathways represent three different urbanization rates: rapid, moderate, and slow. 5. The rapid urbanization pathway assumes the highest population and economic growth rates, while the slow urbanization scenario assumes the lowest rates. The moderate urbanization scenario falls between these two extremes. 6. Urbanisation patterns are dependent on government policies that can either promote or hinder urbanisation rate. Therefore, for a city undertaking emissions modelling and scenario planning, the choice of applying a particular urbanization rate and corresponding population growth rates ultimately rests with the city and state governments. The CRCAP for Vadodara adopts the moderate urbanization scenario. Key performance indicators will be used by the city to track climate actions. Please refer section 9.3 of Vadodara Climate Resilient City Action Plan (Towards a Net-zero Future by 2070), named 'Monitoring & Tracking Progress' \n

This is a target from the City's Climate Action Plan 2.0. California Executive Order S-3-05 established a long-range GHG reduction target of 80% below 1990 levels by 2050. AB 32, the California Global Warming Solutions Act of 2006, required California to reduce statewide GHG emissions to 1990 levels by 2020. AB 32 also directed the Air Resources Board (CARB) to develop and implement regulations that reduce statewide GHG emissions. Many local governments do not have access to sufficient historical data to prepare a 1990 baseline emissions inventory, which would allow local governments to establish reduction targets that exactly mimic the state's own targets. CARB's 2017 Scoping Plan recommends that local agencies establish communitywide GHG reduction goals for local climate action plans that will help California achieve its 2030 target and longer-term goal. The scoping plan notes that it is appropriate to derive evidence-based targets or goals from local emissions sectors and population projections if this process is consistent with the framework used to develop the Statewide targets. CARB also notes that GHG goals and targets should show a downward trend consistent with the statewide objectives. The GHG emissions reductions associated with the measures in the CAP 2.0 are sufficient to exceed the state-level target established by Senate Bill (SB) 32 and meet the City's 2030 climate action target. Cupertino's climate action targets are to:- Reduce the community's per capita GHG emissions to 3.39 MT CO2e per person by 2030, which equals a 50 percent reduction from 2010 per capita levels, or a 66 percent reduction from 1990 per capita levels by 2030.36- Based on projected population growth through 2030, this is equivalent to reducing the community's mass emissions to 222,867 MT CO2e by 2030, or 45 percent below the community's 1990 GHG emissions.- Achieve net-zero MT CO2e per person, or carbon neutrality, by 2040. Maintain carbon neutrality through 2045 and beyond.*Note: 2022 emissions have not yet been assessed. Therefore, the 2018 emissions level was entered as a proxy for 2022 until a more recent inventory is completed. 

The City of Cupertino's GHG reduction targets align with science-based methodologies outlined in the U.S. Community Protocol for Accounting and Reporting Greenhouse Gas Emissions. Our consultant responsible for our 2021 GHG Inventory update and developing our CAP 2.0 targets indicated our long-term, net-zero targets align with the CA state-level climate goals and science-based targets framework. This is consistent with the standards set out by the California Office of Planning and Research (OPR)'s guidance on GHG targets as well.

SBT methodology is explained on page 30 of the CAP 2.0 https://www.cupertino.gov/files/assets/city/v/1/our-community/documents/cupertino-climate-action-p.pdf

column39: The City's 2035 goal of carbon neutrality is aimed at reducing community-wide emissions to 0. However, the path towards carbon neutrality set by the City's 2020 Climate Action Plan would leave approximately 111,030 MTCO2e in annual emissions in 2035 to reduce or offset to achieve true carbon neutrality. Achieving community-wide carbon neutrality is contingent on numerous outside factors, such as increased state funding for climate action, the federal government taking responsibility for climate action and supporting local action, and a regional approach to supporting the clean energy economy. Specifically, this target is conditional on the implementation of SB 100, a California statewide bill requiring that 33% of the electricity sold by a provider by 2020 be renewable, that 60% of electricity be renewable by 2030, and that 100% of all electricity must be carbon-free (although not necessarily renewable) by 2045. Additionally, this target is conditional on the successful implementation of California Title 24 energy efficiency standards for new buildings and clean car standards set by California. This target is also conditional on the community choice aggregation, Central Coast Community Energy, providing 100% carbon free electricity to the community.

column39: For 2019, Antalya's greenhouse gas emission, excluding industry (Emissions specified as excluding industry are greenhouse gas emission values excluding industry, civil airports, fugitive emissions, agriculture and energy production) , has been calculated as 8,232,919tCO2e. With the reduction measures put forward in the sectors, it is planned that Antalya's per capita emissions will decrease from 3.28 tCO2e/person in 2019 to approximately 1.96 tCO2e/person in 2030. It is concluded that with the reduction measures put forward in the sectors, a 40% reduction can be achieved in Antalya's per capita emissions by 2030 compared to 2019. With the BAU (Bussiness As Usual) scenario of Antalya, the predictions made by different institutions regarding the population and sectoral growth were evaluated and the 2030 emissions were calculated as 7.886.537 tCO2e according to this scenario. By 2030, it is aimed to reduce 4,576,943 tCO2e in the buildings sector, 2.009.046 tCO2e in the transportation sector, 923,349 tCO2e in other sectors including waste and wastewater actions, and 377,208 tCO2e with renewable energy. Antalya Sustainable Energy Action Plan creates a roadmap to reduce emissions from energy consumption in different sectors determined with the participation of urban stakeholders. According to the Nationally Determined Intended Contribution (INDC) proposed by Turkey to the UNFCCC, it is recommended to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 21% from the usual course. Turkey approved the Paris Agreement and declared the net zero-carbon target for 2053. Antalya Metropolitan Municipality defined its carbon neutral target as 2050 according to the EU Targets and the Covenant of Mayors. Antalya Metropolitan Municipality is a signatory to the Covenant of Mayors, established by the European Commission to encourage and support urban reduction plans to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from cities and to encourage the use of clean energy sources. In this context, it undertakes to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by at least 40% in 2030 compared to 2019, the base year, and to implement the steps specified in adaptation to climate change.

The quantity of urban GHG emissions across Kadıköy is approximately 1,509,302 tons of CO2e (excluding solid waste) for 2016 which is selected as the reference year. They are followed by emissions from the transportation sector (34% in total), tertiary buildings (14%), the industrial sector (4%), and wastewaterand fugitive emissions (1.5%), respectively. KCAAP presented BAU (Business as Usual) scenario for Kadıköy, using the projections of populationand sectoral growth furnished by several organizations, and calculated 2030 emissions to be approximately 2,247,700 tons of CO2e. The largest component of 2030 emissions is residential buildings (48%) as is in the reference year. The categories of the transportation sector and non-residentialbuildings are expected to be 35% and 13%, respectively.In qualitative and quantitative aspects, the urban growth rate of Turkey is similar to that of cities in developing countries rather than the cities in developed/industrialized countries. As it is impossible to refer to absolute emissions reductions in connection with this rate of growth, it will be a properact to describe emission reduction targets as emissions per capita. Based on the BAU scenario, the emissions per capita is reduced from 3.34 tons of CO2e to 3.18 (5% decrease). As shown in KCAAP, the emissions per capita across Kadıköy can be reduced by approximately 40% in 2030 compared to 2016 with the reduction measures indicated for every sector. https://iklim.kadikoy.bel.tr/Uploads/iklim.kadikoy.bel.tr/202105271202061.pdf (Pages 63-67)

O Roteiro Nacional para a Neutralidade Carbónica 2050 define como meta a redução de emissões entre 85% e 90% até 2050 (face a valores de 2005) e a compensação das restantes emissões.
A Câmara Municipal da Maia traçou um objetivo mais ambicioso de redução em 85% das suas emissões de gases com efeito de estufa até 2030, antecipando a meta de descarbonização prevista a nível nacional através do desenvolvimento do Roteiro para a Neutralidade Carbónica Maia 2030.
Esta ambição supera as metas estabelecidas pela Lei de Bases do Clima (Lei n.º 98/2021, de 31 de dezembro) de redução de emissões de gases de efeito de estufa em, pelo menos, 55%, até 2030, entre 65% e 75% até 2040 e, pelo menos, 90% até 2050, face aos níveis de 2005. 
As emissões referentes ao ano base (2008) totalizavam 963 551tCO2eq e as emissões relatadas em 2021 foram de 744 684 t CO2eq, representando uma redução das emissões na ordem dos 23% face ao ano base. 
Estes valores comprovam que os objetivos nacionais fixados para 2030 estariam quase a ser atingidos a nível local, o que se comprova através dos valores das emissões para o ano 2023, num total de 595 924 tCO2eq, representando uma redução de cerca de 38% das emissões do Município da Maia face ao ano base. 
Importa referir que o método de cálculo das emissões sofreu aperfeiçoamentos e melhorias nos últimos anos e, portanto, estes não são os valores reportados no PAES. Os valores foram atualizados e encontram-se em conformidade com o Roteiro para a Neutralidade Carbónica Maia 2030.

column39:
O Município da Covilhã estabeleceu a meta de reduzir as suas emissões de CO₂ em 55% até 2030, tendo como ano-base 2008. Esta ambição está integrada no Pacto dos Autarcas e alinha-se com os objetivos nacionais e europeus de combate às alterações climáticas e de transição energética para um modelo de baixo carbono. A meta abrange as principais fontes de emissões do território municipal, incluindo os setores residencial, terciário (edifícios e equipamentos), transportes e gestão de resíduos, com especial enfoque na recolha seletiva e no tratamento de biorresíduos.

Para projetar as emissões futuras e acompanhar o progresso, o Município recorre a um inventário detalhado de emissões, utilizando 2008 como referência. A monitorização, realizada anualmente, segue as recomendações do Pacto dos Autarcas e do Joint Research Centre da Comissão Europeia. O método baseia-se em indicadores específicos que avaliam as emissões por setor e por medida, permitindo ajustar as projeções em função da execução das ações previstas e da evolução do mix energético nacional, marcado pelo aumento da incorporação de energias renováveis.

O plano para alcançar a meta inclui diversas ações estratégicas. Destacam-se a modernização da frota de transportes públicos, com a introdução de autocarros elétricos e a criação de uma rede integrada que inclui bicicletas e trotinetes elétricas; o desenvolvimento do Plano de Mobilidade Urbana Sustentável (PMUS), com metas para melhorar a acessibilidade e reduzir as emissões do setor dos transportes; a implementação do projeto “Covilhã Sustentável”, que promove a recolha seletiva de biorresíduos com viaturas 100% elétricas; a certificação energética e reabilitação de edifícios municipais e escolares; a substituição da iluminação pública por tecnologia LED; a instalação de uma rede de carregamento para veículos elétricos em todas as freguesias do concelho; e ações de reflorestação e gestão do arvoredo urbano, com vista à captura de carbono e melhoria da qualidade ambiental.

Até 2023, segundo o 1.º relatório de monitorização, a implementação destas medidas resultou num avanço de 56% no percurso do Município da Covilhã rumo à meta de 2030. Este resultado demonstra o compromisso do Município, que dispõe de um sistema de monitorização e avaliação que permite ajustar as ações com base nos resultados obtidos. Em caso de desvios, prevê-se a revisão das prioridades e o reforço das medidas.

A meta abrange setores fundamentais para a sustentabilidade local e a abordagem integrada do plano permite responder aos desafios da eficiência energética e da descarbonização de forma adaptada às especificidades do território. O envolvimento da população, o apoio ao investimento privado e a promoção de parcerias público-privadas são também considerados essenciais para o sucesso da estratégia.

column39:
A meta de neutralidade carbónica até 2050, estabelecida pelo Município da Covilhã, está alinhada com os compromissos climáticos nacionais e europeus e visa alcançar um balanço zero entre as emissões de gases com efeito de estufa (GEE) produzidas e as removidas da atmosfera. Este objetivo exige uma transição energética profunda, uma redução significativa das emissões em todos os setores e o aumento da capacidade de absorção de carbono pelo território municipal.

Para projetar as emissões até 2050, o Município utiliza um método de modelação baseado em inventários históricos (com ano-base em 2008) e em monitorização contínua, seguindo as orientações do Pacto dos Autarcas e do Joint Research Centre (JRC) da Comissão Europeia. A modelação inclui a análise por setor, como edifícios residenciais e terciários, transportes, gestão de resíduos e espaços verdes, e considera as políticas públicas em vigor, os avanços tecnológicos e as alterações na matriz energética nacional, particularmente o aumento do uso de energias renováveis.

O plano para atingir a neutralidade carbónica assenta na continuidade e reforço das medidas já em curso: expansão da mobilidade elétrica e sustentável, aumento da eficiência energética em edifícios públicos e privados, substituição da iluminação pública por tecnologia LED, promoção da recolha seletiva e valorização de biorresíduos com recurso a viaturas elétricas, e projetos de reflorestação e gestão do arvoredo urbano, fundamentais para a captura de carbono e a resiliência ambiental.

Até 2023, o Município registou um progresso de 34% no caminho para a neutralidade carbónica, com base na implementação das medidas definidas no Plano de Sustentabilidade Energética. A evolução é acompanhada por um sistema de monitorização que permite o ajustamento das estratégias e garante a responsabilização institucional em caso de desvios. A cooperação entre setor público, sociedade civil e setor privado é considerada essencial para assegurar a viabilidade financeira e social do processo.

A meta cobre as principais fontes de emissão no território municipal, com exceção habitual das emissões provenientes da aviação e navegação internacionais. Está centrada na redução das emissões diretas e indiretas associadas ao consumo energético e à gestão dos recursos naturais. Para garantir a sua concretização, o Município compromete-se a definir prioridades anuais de investimento, a promover parcerias público-privadas e a garantir o acesso a mecanismos de financiamento adequados até 2050.

No âmbito da elaboração e aprovação do Pano Municipal de Ação Climática (PMAC) do Município da Figueira da Foz, aprovado em 2023 (que contou com o apoio da Universidade de Coimbra /Instituto de Sistemas e Robótica, no âmbito do Projeto LIFE OwnYourSECAP, e ainda da colaboraçao da Coopérnico - Cooperativa de Energias Renováveis), foi definida uma meta de redução de 59% de emissões de CO2, até 2030 (relativamente ao ano 2019), sendo esta uma meta mais ambiciosa do que a definida no Plano Nacional de Energia e Clima, que estabelece uma redução de 55% de emissões, até 2030 (com o pressuposto naturalmente de obter a neutralidade climática em 2050). Esta meta foi desenvolvida usando a metodologia do OPCC. Ter esta meta dá confiança ao município de que contribuirá com a sua parte, e de forma justa, para as reduções das emissões globais. 

Importa no entanto referir que a meta que consta no PMAC teve em consideração um inventário de emissões efetuado pelo Município, referente a 2019, através de dados fornecidos pelas diversas entidades nacionais competentes (Direção Geral de Energia e Geologia, Instituto Nacional de Estatística, outras). O Município optou por não adotar o inventário de emissões elaborado pela Agência Portuguesa do Ambiente, no PMAC (que se encontra reportado no presente formulário) por duas razões:
- o inventário da APA contempla as emissões das instalações industriais abrangidas pelo Comércio Europeu de Licencas de Emissão (CELE), e o Município não pretendia contemplar essas emissões, tal como recomendação estabelecida pelo Pacto dos Autarcas para a Energia e Clima;
- o inventário da APA não apresenta os dados discriminados, conforme as categorias exigidas no Pacto dos Autarcas para a Energia e Clima

Assim sendo, por forma a excluir do inventário essa tipologia de indústrias abrangidas pelo regime CELE (que apresentam, no Município da Figueira da Foz, quantidades muito significativas de emissões de Gases com Efeito de Estufa), optou-se pelo desenvolvimento de um inventário novo. Este encontra-se apresentado no PMAC (assim como a definição da meta). 
Sobre este ponto importa ainda referir que no inventário constante do PMAC, para efeitos de cálculo das emissões de CO2, optou‐se por utilizar, sempre que possível, os fatores de emissão do IPCC (tal como sugerido pelo Pacto dos Autarcas para o Clima e Energia).

All emissions were compiled in to an emissions inventory, complex modeling was undertaken to produce an emissions reductions pathway to net zero by 2038. 

Number of scenarios were modeled using the Ricardo Net Zero Projections Tool (NZPT) to give sector based actions and activities that need to be taken between now and 2038 to achieve net zero.
The activities and resulting targets form the basis of the Bradford Climate Action Plan (CAP) 2025-2028.
 
The actions withing the CAP were co-created with wide range of stakeholders to develop our Future Ready Pathway to Net Zero. 

The net zero scenario, referred to as the Future-Ready pathway, represents a technically robust and politically realistic trajectory towards Bradford's 2038 climate target. Designed to be ambitious yet feasible, this scenario combines cost-effective interventions with strategic co-benefits, grounded in Bradford's local strengths and challenges. It begins with immediate action and progressively ramps up mitigation efforts through to 2038, utilising a blend of demand reduction, fuel switching, energy efficiency improvements, and enabling measures such as planning, partnerships, and community engagement. This scenario reflects a “no regrets” approach and “best value” pathway that simultaneously reduces emissions, builds local resilience, and unlocks green investment

There is still 18% residual emissions and these will be considered carefully in future iteration of CAP. Looking for opportunities to reduce them further

Cornwall's target is to meet net zero emissions by 2045 with an 88% emission reduction (495922 t Co2e) with remaining 12% emissions to be balanced through increasing biological carbon sequestration e.g. expanding afforestation, improved soil carbon, improved peatland management and blue carbon initiatives.

The emissions included within this target are slightly different to the information stored in other sectors of the CDP form. This SBT is based on an GDP 2012 Expanded scope (additional scope 3 emissions have been added) and sequestration emissions have been removed.

Cornwall Council seeks to acknowledge the scale of emissions reductions required in line with the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities for Cornwall to contribute our fair-share toward a science-based, Paris Agreement-compliant decarbonisation pathway.

Emissions calculated using latest data year of 2022 as 2025 not yet available.

column39: In 2019, North Tyneside Council declared a climate emergency. This declaration set a target to reduce the carbon footprint of the Council's operations, and the borough, by 50% by 2023 and to align to the Government's net zero target of 2050. This aimed to build on the excellent work we had already undertaken to enhance and protect our environment. During 2020 we worked with industry experts The Carbon Trust and consulted with a wide range of stakeholders in the production of our 'Climate Emergency Action Plan'. The Carbon Trust action plan, available here (and attached): https://democracy.northtyneside.gov.uk/documents/s4552/Climate%20Emergency%20Update%20-%20North%20Tyneside%20Climate%20Emergency%20Action%20Plan-Appendix.pdf set out emissions scenario analyses to help the Borough understand how it may be able to meet its net-zero target. Four scenarios were produced: 'Business as usual', 'Energy efficiency and alternative fuels', 'High electrification' and 'Radical response'. The scenarios achieve a 26%, 86%, 85% and 94% reduction in emissions respectively from the 2017 baseline to the target year in 2050, with a variety of interim targets / pathways :Starting from North Tyneside's 2019 footprint, the report projects emissions over the 30 year period from 2020-2050 to determine five-yearly budgets for the Council aligned to either a 1.5°C pathway, a net zero target or the UK's CCC 5-yearly budgets. All of the carbon budgets presented are aligned with or are more ambitious than the science-based targets calculated by the Tyndall Centre: https://carbonbudget.manchester.ac.uk/reports/E08000022/The Council has been delivering against the strategic actions in that plan to drive down carbon emissions. However, in light of rising global emissions and the evidence of the need to take significant action well in advance of the 2050 target to limit global warming to well below 2oC, Council published a new ambitious policy commitment in 'Our North Tyneside Plan Council Plan 2021- 25', committing the authority to the publishing of an action plan of the steps we will take and the national investment we will seek to make North Tyneside carbon net zero by 2030 - see the action plan attached. Please note: UK Gov's GHG inventory for local authorities has been retrospectively updated to include more emissions streams, such as waste. As such, the emissions baseline has been amended to reflect the recent changes

column39: This is a science-based target. The 2041 target also includes an interim target of a 33% carbon emission reduction by 2026 (against a 2016 baseline). This came from the Tyndall Centre report (the UK target is now 100% reduction in GHGs by 2050, but the WMCA target still exceeds it): The WMCA's Five Year Plan, published in 2021, outlined how under a highly ambitious 'Accelerated' scenario, goals in domestic, commercial, industrial, transport and land use sectors could deliver a 33% reduction by 2026 (against 2016 baseline) and net zero by 2041. The “Accelerated” scenario is to be used as the standard to set the delivery goal ambitions.The UK Climate Change Act 2008 legislates a commitment to at least an 80% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 from 1990 levels, with five yearly carbon budgets to set actions and review progress. However, the level of these budgets is not aligned to the Paris Agreement. The WMCA target goes beyond the ambition of the 2008 Climate Change Act, the current recommendations of the UK Government's advisory body the Committee on Climate Change (CCC). This is primarily due to two key differences between our approach and that of the CCC to date:a) The equity principles of the Paris Agreement and wider UNFCCC process are explicitly and quantitatively applied. Our approach allocates a smaller share of the global carbon budget to the 'developed country Parties', such as the UK, relative to 'developing country Parties'. b) Carbon removals via negative emissions technologies (NETs) are not included. The CCC include a significant role for NETs such as bioenergy carbon capture and storage and direct air capture in their analysis. Doing so increases the size of a carbon budget compatible with a given global temperature target. However carbon removal technologies are at a very early stage of development and whether they can be successfully deployed at sufficient scale is highly uncertain. These sub-national carbon budgets are therefore more precautionary than the current advice from the Committee on Climate Change.The UK carbon budget to be at the upper end of the range that is aligned with the Paris Agreement's objectives. Early results from the latest Earth system models suggest that the climate may be more sensitive to greenhouse gases than previously thought implying a smaller global carbon budget is required. In addition, assuming that developing countries will, on aggregate, implement rapid emissions reduction measures in line with a 2025 peak year is far from certain. Therefore, we recommend that these sub-national budgets are taken as reflective of the minimum commitment required to deliver on the Paris Agreement.The results in Tyndall report show that for WMCA to make its fair contribution to delivering the Paris Agreement's commitment to staying well below 2°C and pursuing 1.5°C” global temperature rise, then an immediate and rapid programme of decarbonisation is needed. Based on our analysis, for WMCA to make its 'fair' contribution towards the Paris Climate Change Agreement, WMCA needs to reach zero or near zero carbon no later than 2041 and have reduced emissions by 33% by 2026. This report provides two CO2 reduction pathways which both stay within the recommended 126 MtCO2 carbon budget; 1) with a long term decay in residual emissions at a consistent percentage reduction rate over time, 2) emissions dropping to zero following the point at which 95% of the budget has been used. Data on the covered emissions in most recent inventory and the year the target was established are sourced from (please note this is different from the Scatter data used for 3.1.1 because this provides a more up-to-date total figure): https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/uk-local-authority-and-regional-greenhouse-gas-emissions-statistics-2005-to-2022

Principles of Greenhouse Gas Reduction Target Setting
Yasothon Town Municipality has adopted a greenhouse gas reduction target using a (Base-Year Emissions Goal) approach. This approach establishes a (Single-year Goal) for reducing greenhouse gas emissions compared to the base year emissions. The target is set to achieve at least a 20% reduction by 2027 compared to 2022 (base year) emissions through three phases of implementation measures:

- Short-term Measures
These measures require minimal investment capital with an expected payback period of 1-2 years. They can be implemented using either the organization's regular budget or through next year's budget allocation. Success in this phase requires a clear understanding of cost-effectiveness, delivered through municipal training programs and seminars.

- Medium-term Measures
These measures involve moderate capital investment, such as installing energy-efficient electrical systems, with an expected payback period of 2-5 years. These measures primarily target the business sector, including hotels and large enterprises, focusing on upgrading to high-efficiency or energy-saving electrical equipment.

- Long-term Measures
These measures require substantial investment and clear budget planning, with payback periods exceeding 5 years. Examples include installing solar power systems to replace grid electricity. While these measures may have longer payback periods of 8-10 years, they provide energy savings benefits for 20-25 years.

Based on our current operational plan, we have not included provisions for purchasing offset credits from external sources.

This action plan identifies GHG mitigation targets for 2025 (short term targets), 2027 (intermediate targets) and 2030 (End Target).

Bhavnagar's Net Zero CRCAP aims to make the city climate-resilient and advance towards net zero emissions. It proposes strategies such as promoting energy efficiency in buildings, increasing RE use, adopting sustainable waste management practices, and encouraging low-carbon transport options. Bhavnagar's Climate Resilient City Action Plan (CRCAP) has been developed using the ClimateResilientCITIES methodology. This includes guidance for baseline analyses and identification, and prioritization of climate resilient strategies and targets.

Scenario Planning, a critical step in the process of developing an ambitious climate action plan, establishes the business as usual (BAU) future emissions trajectory. Emissions reduction strategies, scales of action and multiple targets are defined and analysed to arrive at the Low Emission Growth Scenario.

BAU Projection: The BAU projection shows the level of GHG emissions that would result in the future if the current levels and patterns of climate action are followed. It assumes that no additional emissions reduction efforts and measures will be undertaken, beyond those already in place. The BAU projection represents the 'baseline condition' and serves as a reference point for assessing the impact of emissions reduction scenarios or pathways.

The Low Emission Growth Scenario: It builds on and aligns with the broader frameworks and initiatives at both national and state levels, incorporating local strategies and actions to advance GHG emissions reduction. This scenario aligns with the targets, goals, and guidelines set by national and state governments through various policies, plans, missions, programs, and schemes. Additionally, it considers existing/planned/proposed projects and policies approved by the city government. Compared to the baseline status, this scenario aims for higher levels of action and more ambitious targets, while considering on-ground realities, local context, available resources, and existing constraints.

Guiding Principles for estimating the BAU scenario:
1. The relationship between the quantum of emissions and the rate of urbanization is assumed to be directly proportional.
2. Urbanization rate is influenced by the population and economic growth, which are affected by interdependent factors such as secondary and tertiary sector growth, education levels, birth and death rates, life expectancy, and migration.
3. Urbanization refers to expanding urban centres in terms of geographical area and population, driven by shifts in the economy from primary to secondary, tertiary, or quaternary activities.
4. For modelling of the projected BAU emissions, three different urbanization pathways have been evaluated based on the UN's World Urbanisation Prospects methodologies, the IPCC-endorsed Shared Socio-economic Pathways, and guidance from the Global Cities Institute. These pathways represent three different urbanization rates: rapid, moderate, and slow.
5. The rapid urbanization pathway assumes the highest population and economic growth rates, while the slow urbanization scenario assumes the lowest rates. The moderate urbanization scenario falls between these two extremes.
6. Urbanisation patterns are dependent on government policies that can either promote or hinder urbanisation rate. Therefore, for a city undertaking emissions modelling and scenario planning, the choice of applying a particular urbanization rate and corresponding population growth rates ultimately rests with the city and state governments. The CRCAP for Bhavnagar adopts the moderate urbanization scenario.

column39: The development of the Whitby Climate Emergency Response Plan (CERP) has been identified as the primary mechanism to respond to a changing climate across the community and is being completed in two phases:• Climate Emergency Response Plan: Phase 1: Resilience (completed in 2022).• Climate Emergency Response Plan: Phase 2: Mitigation (in the final stages of development)A Whitby specific CERP was established to identify, prioritize, and cost, at a project level, actions that address climate change within the municipality. Both Phase 1 & 2 of the plan will be informed by the work already completed at a Regional level, however CERP was developed leveraging the latest scientific data such as updated regional climate projections and global greenhouse gas emission projections. Climate Emergency Response Plan: Phase 2: Mitigation Phase 2 of the Whitby's Climate Emergency Response Plan is currently underway with an anticipated completion date of October 2023. This plan will include the following key deliverables:• Community wide GHG inventory report for the Town of Whitby;• Spatial layers modelling energy consumption and emissions on a neighbourhood scale;• Climate Change Mitigation Strategy;• Climate Change Mitigation Implementation and Action Plan; and,• Engagement Summary Report. Baseline Year: The baseline year for the energy and emissions consumed is 2020 which represents a 5-year update of the Region's original inventory. The future year is 2050 which aligns with Regional, Provincial and Federal emission reduction timelines. CityInsight was used to develop the greenhouse gas emissions inventory, the consultant leveraged the City Insight Model. This model allows Whitby to generate a community energy and emissions model with integrated spatially explicit land-use and transportation components, and stocks-and-flows accounting and actual energy consumption data. To understand what emissions could look like in the future, three scenarios will be developed:1. Business as Usual (BAU)Through the BAU scenario, a greenhouse gas pathway to the year 2050 is developed considering current patterns of energy consumption, while accounting for population growth, fuel efficiency standards and the impacts of climate change on heating and cooling requirements in buildings.2. Business as Planned (BAP)The BAP scenario projects emissions based on an anticipated increase in provincial building codes, building retrofits in the residential and commercial sectors (considering current policy directives such as the Whitby Green Standard), adoption of building scale solar photovoltaic systems, electric vehicles and a modest increase in local large-scale solar and wind generation.3. Low Carbon Pathway (LCP)The LCP will be developed to achieve Whitby's community greenhouse gas reduction targets. This model will evaluate different actions such as building efficiency standards, building retrofits, renewable energy, technological advancement, electrification of transportation, land-use changes, and industrial efficiencies to determine which actions will need to be implemented to reach the community's targets. All three scenarios consider all forms of energy including supply, demand, storage, and transmittal. The energy system and the community priorities relating to energy have been modelled whilst considering future considerations such as: population growth, land use, economic growth; and, the development of sustainable communities. Work completed to date suggests that the Town of Whitby must consider adopting a community-wide greenhouse gas emission reduction target of net zero by 2045. This target was developed to reflect the community's contribution to limiting the global annual average temperature increase to 1.5°C based on the International Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) . Globally, to remain under the 1.5 degree threshold, there is only a capacity for 600 Gigatons of emissions to be released from the year 2021-2050. This is the global carbon budget. Applying an equity-based target, by taking into consideration both historic and future emissions, Whitby globally has consumed to date more emissions than those of developing nations. Whitby is committing to ramping down its greenhouse gas emissions at a slightly more accelerated rate to enable developing nations to maintain emissions in the short term, so that climate action does not add to the challenges of addressing global poverty and energy security. This equity-based target is derived through a method developed by an organization called the Science-Based Target Network (SBTN), which is a network of 45+ global organizations developing methods and resources to identify science and equity-based targets. In September 2022, through an interim report on Phase 2: Mitigation Plan of CERP, Council approved the following targets: Council Approved Targets Community GHG emission reductions targets (below 2020 levels)o 20 % by 2025o 40 % by 2030o 100 %by 2045
